title: Fan-built roller-coaster sets new standard in match-day choreography
text:
Tifo displays have long been a ubiquitous sight in football stadiums around the world.

Typically displayed before kick-off at major matches, fan-led displays have become increasingly elaborate as rival supporters look to outdo one another with the scale of their devotion.

But German second-tier side VfL Osnabrück have taken things to an entirely new level.

Ahead of their German Cup tie against defending champions Bayern Munich, the supporters created a fully functioning roller-coaster in the stands of their 16,100-capacity stadion an der Bremer Brücke.

VfL Osnabrück fans truly surpassed themselves on this occasion. (Getty Images: Lars Baron)

A track was built in sections and had a cart, complete with dummy passengers, which was towed around the track on repeat.

To one side of the stand, a separate "photo" banner was displayed after the cart passed a flashing camera, delivering the authentic experience of what the supporters called the "Funpark Bremer Brücke".

Loading Instagram content

Accompanied by a sign saying "VfL Osnabrück — a roller-coaster ride!" the not-so-subtle message was that supporting the club, based in Germany's north-western Saxony region, was full of ups and downs.

The club has only just been promoted back to the 2. Bundesliga after a five-year stint in the 3. Liga and has a reputation as a club that yo-yos around the leagues.

VfL Osnabrück brought the pyro to their party against Bayern Munich. (Getty Images: picture alliance/David Ebener)

Welcoming Bavarian giants Bayern in the first round of the DFB Pokal was always going to be a tough ask, but the roller-coaster theme continued when the hosts took a shock 1-0 lead thanks to a 30-yard shot by Robin Meißner after just five minutes.

The defending champions soon hit back though, Harry Kane scoring twice either side of goals to Tom Bischof and Michael Olise to give the record 21-time winners a path through to the second round.

But Bayern, who are not strangers to spectacular tifos of their own at their cavernous Allianz Arena home, will have to up their game if they are to manage something as impressive as this for their next home game, against Bodø/Glimt in the Champions League.

Bayern are partial to the odd display of mass choreography. (Getty Images: sampics/Stefan Matzke)

Germany has been something of a trendsetter when it comes to tifos in recent years, although the practice originated in southern Europe and Italy.

Starting out as supporters holding up cards to create a display across a grandstand, Australian fans can think of a tifo as something similar to the fan-made banners AFL teams run through pre-game, only on a much larger scale.

Tifo is short for tifosi, the Italian for supporter, and has become known as a way for fans to display their passion or to mock their rivals.

Tifos originated in Italy, with San Siro home to some of the best. (Getty Images: AC Milan/Diego Puletto)

In 2017, Western Sydney Wanderers provoked the ire of Football Australia, then known as Football Federation Australia, for displaying a homophobic banner during the Sydney derby.

The banner, depicting a blue-faced man giving oral sex, was put up in the Wanderers' support area during the second half of the game.

"FFA is aware of the unauthorised and totally unacceptable banner that was displayed in the Western Sydney Wanderers area during Saturday night's Sydney derby at ANZ Stadium," then-A-League chief Greg O'Rourke said.

"The discriminatory nature of the tifo has no place in society and will not be tolerated in the A-League."

Not all of Western Sydney Wanderers' tifos were vile, most were excellent. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Clubs can play a role in the content of tifos, but often they are ways for fans to make their point about an issue they feel strongly about.

Given the increasingly elaborate designs, Arsenal were heavily criticised by their own fans for a bland rectangular tifo ahead of a Champions League match at the Emirates against Paris Saint-Germain in April 2025.

PSG are known for their extravagant displays — particularly in the Champions League — so perhaps it was fair for Arsenal to be mocked.

Paris Saint-Germain fans are increasingly keen on displaying tifos. (Getty Images: UEFA/Stuart Franklin)

However, since then they have upped their game significantly.

Still, we're yet to see a roller-coaster of any sort at the Emirates, so there's clearly still room for improvement.

As fans of Lechia Gdansk know, the devil is often in the detail. (Getty Images: Mateusz Slodkowski)

title: Canberra woman to receive $100k settlement over illegal strip search
text:
The ACT government has agreed to pay a Canberra woman $100,000 after her human rights were breached during an illegal strip search at Canberra's jail.

Aboriginal woman Julianne Williams sued the territory in July over her treatment while she was detained at the Alexander Maconochie Centre (AMC) in 2021.

During a civil case against the ACT government last year, the ACT Supreme Court found she was subjected to an attempted strip search in her room, and a strip search in the toilet, and both had breached the Human Rights Act.

The use of force by officers was also incompatible with Ms Williams's human right to humane and appropriate treatment, Justice Verity McWilliam said in her decision late last year.

The lead-up to the strip search was captured on the prison's CCTV and guards' body-worn camera footage.

The footage showed Ms Williams in a state of distress after learning that the prison had refused to let her attend her grandmother's funeral.

Loading...

At the time, Ms Williams did not seek compensation from the territory, but the ABC this week reported that she had lodged fresh proceedings in the Federal Court after her application for an act of grace from the ACT government stalled.

Her statement of claim showed she was seeking compensatory damages intended to act to both rectify the pain caused and deter the territory from similar behaviour in the future.

Court orders seen by the ABC show the government settled the matter with Ms Williams on Thursday, agreeing to pay her $100,000 plus costs as assessed between the parties.

The Alexander Maconochie Centre is Canberra's only prison and has about 450 detainees. (ABC News: Michael Black)

The ACT government said act of grace applications were assessed on their merits in accordance with legal frameworks, and did not comment on individual decisions.

ACT Corrective Services said the AMC had removed mandatory strip searches from its procedures in 2022, and introduced body scanners in 2023.

Commissioner Leanne Close told ABC Radio Canberra that before body scanners, more than 4,000 strip searches were conducted at the AMC in the years 2020 and 2021.

"After the introduction, in 2024, we've reduced that down to 580 strip searches," Ms Close said.

But she said it would not reduce the need for strip searches entirely, in the event of anomalies, weapons or illicit drugs being detected.

ACT Corrective Services said it was also introducing an additional body scanner at the Court Transport Unit.

"We've also strengthened staff training, guidance and oversight to support consistent, human-rights-based decision-making in a complex custodial environment," a spokesperson said.

title: Five hospitalised after forklift catches fire in Brisbane
text:
A person has sustained life-threatening burns in a blaze at a commercial site in Brisbane's east.

A forklift caught alight at a business on Anton Road at Hemmant at about 11am.

Firefighters are working to stop the flames spreading to nearby shipping containers.

A forklift caught alight at a business on Anton Road at Hemmant at about 11am. (ABC News)

One patient has life-threatening burns to their chest, head and face, while another has suffered serious burns to their arms.

Emergency services say three people are being treated for smoke inhalation.

All five are being transported to hospital.

title: Shifting Ayrton Senna plaque a sign of things to come for Adelaide's MotoGP
text:
A plaque installed after F1 driver Ayrton Senna died in 1994 is among a swag of changes to Adelaide's famed street circuit for the MotoGP next year, but an industry stalwart says it represents "transition" rather than the end of an era.

The government wants to return parts of the circuit to its original F1 layout, including the 900-metre Brabham Straight along Dequetteville Terrace, but is also proposing to shift Senna Chicane further into Victoria Park and dump popular Supercar components.

This includes the "staircase" and its challenging succession of 90-degree turns along the CBD's east edge.

"It's a new life, a different life for one of the best locations for a motor racing circuit in Australia," said Motorsport Hall of Fame chairman and longtime industry journalist John Smailes.

The Senna Chicane is a historic turn in the Adelaide Street Circuit that harkens back to the F1 days. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"It still sits in Victoria Park where [track designer] Bob Barnard placed it in 1985, so you're talking about a rich 41-year history of Victoria Park hosting probably the best Grand Prix that's ever been held in the Southern Hemisphere for cars.

"It's so close to town; it really does involve the whole city and, to that end, whatever the layout may happen to be, the geography remains pretty much the same."

A popular circuit

After the Grand Prix moved to Melbourne in 1996, the circuit was reduced to 3.2 kilometres for the 1999 Adelaide 500, which became the most well-attended leg of the Supercars Championship and grew a reputation for challenging corners, bumps and upsets.

Loading...

One of the Adelaide street circuit's major drawcards, however, is that spectators can be seated close to the action for much of the course.

The MotoGP, on the other hand, requires very large gravel traps along the far edge of corners to slow a dismounted rider safely, meaning spectators will be set a significant way back for bigger stretches of the circuit.

Mr Smailes pointed out there were parts of the current Phillip Island MotoGP course where "you can get up close and personal with the bikes", and expected the same in Adelaide.

The proposed MotoGP street has wide gravel pits along much of the course. (Supplied: SA government)

Viewing areas for the current Adelaide street circuit are largely close to the action. (Supplied: Daniel Kalisz)

"There'll probably be places where the aficionados will scope out the best parts to stand where they can still get the buzz of being close," Mr Smailes said.

" And when you cop the full force of a 320 kilometre-per-hour MotoGP bike pushing the air in front of you, it's like being hit by a glove from a heavyweight boxer. It's amazing. "

The state government said the MotoGP track will be reconfigured for the Supercars Grand Final, which will take place about 10 days later.

Five-time Supercars champion Mark Skaife said the kerbs would remain "punishing and the walls will be inches away".

"The new Senna Chicane will be unforgiving," he said, and the track will be "super quick, with lots of overtaking opportunities".

MotoGP bikes are expected to hit speeds of 340 kilometres per hour on the Adelaide Street Circuit. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

A larger sticking point

The MotoGP's larger footprint, however, is behind its most controversial sticking point for a lot of Adelaideans, which is its requirement to remove trees from the city's national heritage-listed Parklands.

Angered by tree removals for a revamped golf course, a large protest movement has emerged that marched in the thousands on August 23, while a petition of 43,784 signatures tabled in state parliament has triggered an inquiry.

The state government has responded by promising to replace every tree 10 to one, and arguing that of 377 trees that needed removal, 42 were significant, 88 would be transplanted, and the rest were either "unregulated, invasive species, dead or in poor health".

A protest against tree felling for the MotoGP in late August drew thousands of people. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Mr Smailes believed the issue was of bigger consideration than Senna's memorial plaque.

"I don't think Ayrton Senna would be at all concerned if you moved his plaque to another place. I think that's a very small consideration," he said.

A spokesperson for the South Australian Motor Sport Board said the plaque "commemorating the life of three-time World Champion Ayrton Senna was a part of the folklore of the Adelaide Circuit".

The plaque is currently located adjacent Senna Chicane in Victoria Park. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"The intention is to keep it adjacent to the Senna Chicane, but the exact location won't be determined until the consultation process has concluded and the final circuit design is confirmed," he said.

A 'spectacle for sure'

Adelaide motorsport fan, Simon, told the ABC he was a "car guy, but the MotoGP is probably the most exciting motorsport to watch at the moment, given F1 has become so sanitised and tech-driven", and he would most certainly be attending.

"I'd prefer the F1 to come back, but MotoGP is a spectacle for sure and has a huge global following," he said.

"I also like the fact the infrastructure could be used for the Adelaide Motorsport Festival [AMF] as well, and could see that event become Australia's answer to the Goodwood Festival of Speed [England].

"[AMF owner/CEO] Tim Possingham is a very switched-on guy and I'm sure he has a vision for the AMF to grow and succeed."

A map showing the design for the MotoGP street circuit in Adelaide. (Supplied: SA government)

Mr Possingham said he had been in constant communication with the state government about the incoming MotoGP and was working with it closely with respect to its build times and how the AMF would fit in.

Adelaide MotoGP circuit gets lukewarm motorsport review Adelaide's new $96 million MotoGP track has received mixed reviews from motorsport fans and riders.

"We're also mindful that the Formula One calendar hasn't been released yet, so there's a couple of moving parts we need to fit in with," he said.

"Anything that remotely comes to look like the great track we had in the 80s and the 90s and, in some way, shape or form, brings back that grandeur of a truly international event here in the city of Adelaide is very, very powerful.

"I think that that will be realised maybe after a year or two of the event being delivered here, and I think there's some foresight there of what might come in the future, and the government's looking further afield than national events with MotoGP."

Works have begun for the Adelaide Street Circuit in its current configuration for the final time. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

A public consultation period for the proposed MotoGP track is open until September 20.

title: Bathla creditors' meeting hears company owes $3.4 billion
text:
At Bathla's first creditors' meeting, administrator Teneo said it was in "positive discussions" with five lenders over funding to keep construction going, with Monday morning the key deadline.

Teneo senior managing director Stephen Longley said in the virtual call that he hoped to have the funding arrangements in place by the end of today, but they were giving themselves until Monday morning.

If the five lenders provide funding, construction on their sites can continue, but administrators say they "probably won't be able to support" construction on sites whose lenders are not participating.

Bathla Group has been teetering on the brink of collapse. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Administrators estimate supporting construction would cost the business about $1 million to $1.3 million a week, depending on which projects continue.

Bathla is one of Sydney's biggest residential property developers, with a large pipeline of housing projects and land holdings across the region.

The group was placed into voluntary administration last week after running into severe cashflow problems, leaving administrators to work out which projects can keep operating and how creditors will be repaid.

Much of Bathla's development activity is financed project by project through separate lenders, which has made it difficult to find a single funding solution for the broader business.

Company's debt and property position revealed

Bathla Group owes known creditors about $3.4 billion, based on preliminary figures.

The vast majority ($3.08 billion) is owed to secured lenders.

Bathla also owes about $145 million to the Australian Taxation Office, $42 million in land tax and $130 million to other unsecured creditors.

About $4 million is owed to employees for wages and superannuation.

Administrators also put the preliminary stated value of Bathla's 219 sites at about $4.9 billion.

But Teneo has said the $4.9 billion is not cash available to pay creditors. Much of that value is tied up in land and developments, which can take time to sell, and the valuations are preliminary and still being checked.

Much of Bathla's property is also financed by individual lenders. That means proceeds from a property sale will likely need to go towards that project or its lender, rather than being available to fund the broader Bathla business.

Administrators also said that about $400 million worth of property was currently for sale or under contract, but no cash from that was expected to flow to the group in the near term.

Bathla Group is struggling to survive. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Customer deposits

There were also a number of questions from people attending the meeting about the status of customer deposits.

Administrators said they were still carrying out a full reconciliation, with deposits spread across trust accounts held by multiple law firms.

They confirmed not all customer deposits were sitting in trust accounts, because some sale contracts allowed part of the deposit to be used by the business to fund projects.

However, administrators said some contracts had still settled this week even where the deposits were not held in trust.

title: 'Supermodel' bull sells for $420k, smashing Australian record
text:
An Angus bull from New South Wales has become the most expensive beef animal ever traded in Australia, selling for $420,000 at a Central West bull sale.

Wyatt W50 was just the fourth lot to sell at Millah Murrah's annual sale near Bathurst, where bidding saw the price skyrocket past the former all-breeds bull record of $360,000.

It also surpassed the all-time beef animal record of $400,000 paid for a Wagyu heifer in 2022.

The bull was named after stud principal Ross Thompson's late father, which made the sale emotional for his family.

"I did have sunnies on, but apparently you could see [the tears] streaming," Mr Thompson said.

"He was just simply outstanding and extremely hard to fault. I did consider him the best bull, on balance, that we'd ever put in the sale ring.

"I was wondering why I was selling him by the time we got to the sale."

Auctioneer Paul Dooley said it was an exciting afternoon.

"You can hear the buzz in the crowd as the numbers go up," he said.

"It certainly speaks to the confidence in the cattle industry."

Million-dollar semen sales

Gundungarra Angus purchased the bull at Moss Vale in the NSW Southern Highlands.

In breeding terms, the bull holds genes for everything cattle farmers chase — from calving ease to strong weight gains.

"In human terms, he's supermodel-level looks," Mr Thompson said.

"He's got a pedigree that's globally very diverse and on top of that. He's just an incredibly versatile bull."

The Thompson family, pictured in 2023, has set a number of industry records over the stud's almost 60 year history. (ABC Rural: Hamish Cole )

Millah Murrah retains a 20 per cent share in the bull, and will work closely with Gundungarra Angus to manage the high demand for semen sales.

Mr Thompson said semen from the bull was already attracting interest from Australia, Canada and the USA.

"It's nice to think that people from other parts of the world are looking at Australia as a potential genetic source, so it's quite an exciting moment," he said.

" The semen revenue potential in a bull like that would go into the seven-figure mark. "

Mr Thompson said managing such a valuable animal could be stressful.

"I've got 250 [semen] units in the tank, so if he drops dead, we've got him genetically away," he said.

After a mass sell-off of cattle from drought-hit northern NSW, 2026 was tipped to be a challenging bull-selling season.

But Mr Thompson said the record-breaking bull was in a league of his own.

"You're talking about one particularly elite animal," he said.

title: De Minaur crashes out of US Open in shock straight sets loss
text:
Alex de Minaur has been dumped out of the US Open in the second round, falling in straight sets to Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp 6-4, 7-5, 6-2 in two hours and 43 minutes.

De Minaur had never lost to the 30-year-old world number 70 in their previous four meetings, including earlier this year at the Rotterdam ATP event, which the 27-year-old Aussie won.

But on a night where he committed 29 unforced errors to van de Zandschulp's 21, as well as seven double faults in a sub-par serving display, the Australian world number seven faltered badly.

"I always had really difficult matches against Alex," van de Zandschulp said on court.

"Some tough ones as well, some close matches, but today I served very well, I think that was the difference today."

Alex de Minaur was far from his best. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

De Minaur saved three match points in the final game, but it was not enough, the Aussie leaving himself far too much to do.

After a brief pause where he stood on court in contemplation at his exit, de Minaur exited without looking back.

The defeat is de Minaur's earliest exit at the US Open in five years, at a slam where he has three times reached the quarterfinals.

With Novak Djokovic and Félix Auger-Aliassime both crashing out, de Minaur had been the fourth-highest seed left in the tournament.

But he was unable to make that opportunity count.

Sweeny soars into US Open last 32 Australian wildcard Dane Sweeny has posted the biggest win of his career, upsetting dual grand slam semifinalist Lorenzo Musetti to make the US Open's last 32.

De Minaur was forced to wait until day four to get his tournament underway after rain caused the postponement of his round one clash with Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri.

The victory is van de Zandschulp's second over a top-10 player during this US hardcourt swing after he beat world number eight Daniil Medvedev at the Montreal Masters in August.

The one-time US Open quarterfinalist has made a habit of pulling off shock victories at Flushing Meadows.

He beat Casper Ruud on his way to the quarterfinal in 2021 and, in 2024, knocked out third-seed Carlos Alcaraz in the second round with a straight-sets win.

De Minaur's exit means wildcard Dane Sweeny is the only Australian left in the men's singles draw at Flushing Meadows after his 3-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-2 victory against world number 14 Lorenzo Musetti.

title: More than 100 motorbikes tear through outback pub in world record attempt
text:
The sound of revving engines echoed around the centre of Alice Springs last night as dozens of riders attempted to set the record for the most motorbikes ridden through a pub.

From the leather-clad to the board-short-wearing and everything in between, the riders on commuters and muscle bikes fell just short of their goal at Bojangles Saloon.

Aiming for 125 bikes, only 107 rode through the outback pub, filling it with fumes and noise, as dozens lined the barricades to get a glimpse of the action.

This year's Finke Desert Race motorbike race winner David Walsh, also known as the King of the Desert, led the charge.

Finke Desert Race champion David Walsh led the ride. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

"I was a little bit nervous to be honest," he said.

"It was really cool, something different, it was a great atmosphere, I'm pumped that I did it."

The record attempt was part of Red CentreNATS, the Northern Territory sister festival to Canberra's Summernats, with dozens of car and motorbike events planned over the next few days.

"Alice Springs is full of revheads, there's a lot of nice cars out here so it's cool that we all get to display them … it's just such an amazing event," Mr Walsh said.

Laura Johnson from Red CentreNATS said despite the failed attempt, the fact they even gave it a go was a win.

Bojangles Saloon welcomed the motorbikes, which filled the pub with fumes and noise. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"It might not be a world record, but it is absolutely a record for us and the growth that we've shown from last year, I am so confident that at Red CentreNATS [next year] we are going to smash it out of the park," she said.

She said the atmosphere was electric and Alice Springs locals and volunteers were part of what made Red CentreNATS so great.

"Where else do you shut down the centre of town and ride motorbikes through a pub," she said.

"To be able to be a part of it, for 107 bikes to ride through a venue, that's amazing."

Many riders came from interstate to be a part of the action.

Harley Hall says he will be back next year to try again. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Ngarrindjeri Kokatha-Wirangu man Harley Hall arrived in Alice Springs from South Australia with his family as part of the 3% motorbike group — which he said represented the 3 per cent Indigenous population of Australia.

"That was an adrenaline rush and a half," he said.

" We'll be back next year, we're going to bring more fellas — hopefully we beat the world record. "

Behind the bar after the fog of fumes had lifted, Bojangles Saloon owner Pearl Randhay said she was grateful to have events like Red CentreNATS come to town and bring it to life.

"It was so exciting, I was nervous in a good way, I'm happy everything went well," she said.

Pearl Randhay says the record attempt was exciting. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"Thank goodness we had earplugs."

The event raised money for the Butterfly Connection, an organisation helping central Australians travel interstate for medical treatment.

title: 'Death by a thousand cuts' as mining companies use planning 'loophole'
text:
Coalmining companies in NSW are using loopholes in planning laws to get expansions approved, say the Greens and environmental groups.

Up to 30 million tonnes of additional coal will be extracted from Idemitsu's Boggabri mine after the NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (DPHI) endorsed a modification to the existing plan on Monday.

The decision will keep the New England mine running until 2040, generating an estimated 68 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions.

The modfication will see 84 hectares of native vegetation cleared within the Leard State Forest. (ABC News: Lisa Herbert)

The Greens and environmental groups have accused the NSW government of using the modification process to get around more stringent planning rules for new developments.

Community group People for the Plains (PFTP) was one of 16 objectors to the Boggabri mine modification.

PFTP secretary Sally Hunter said applying for modifications was a "loophole" that mining companies could exploit to avoid the full rigour of applying for a new development.

"Within the NSW planning process, there are certain criteria that need to be met to go through a full process, and these modifications slip under that trigger point," she said.

Sally Hunter believes the state government is allowing mining companies to use "loopholes". (Supplied: Lock the Gate)

"When it goes to a full process, there's a lot more scrutiny, whereas the modifications are reviewed and approved by the department."

Modifications unlocking mining

So far, the government has approved 13 extensions since the 2023 election, including at Mount Pleasant in the Upper Hunter last month.

Greens spokesperson for the environment and climate change Sue Higginson said modifications approved in the Gunnedah basin, the Hunter Valley, and the Upper Hunter were an easy route to unlock more mining.

"It's get in the door, get your approval and then seek the expansion and impact process by modification," she said.

"It's a bit like the death by a thousand cuts analogy.

"Everybody knows we are talking about new coal, new areas for longer periods of time."

Sue Higginson says mine modifications are a slow death. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

The Idemitsu expansion at Boggabri will allow about 84 hectares of native vegetation within the Leard State Forest to be cleared.

PFTP argued the mine would negatively impact the habitat of critically endangered birds such as the regent honeyeater and swift parrot.

Regent honeyeaters are under threat in the region. (Supplied: Dean Ingwersen)

'A full merit-based assessment'

In a statement, Planning Minister Paul Scully said there was no basis for the assertions of loopholes.

"Every mining proposal or modification goes through a full merit-based assessment," he said.

"The modification for Boggabri was on public exhibition from 13 June to 11 July 2025 to allow the community to have their say."

NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully says there is no basis for the assertions of loopholes. (Four Corners)

A DPHI spokesperson said it undertook a rigorous merit assessment of the Boggabri mine, including community input, consideration of greenhouse gas emissions and potential impacts to threatened species, surface water and groundwater.

In the notice of decision, the department imposed several conditions, including reviews and updates of biodiversity and water management plans, and a requirement to prepare a greenhouse mitigation plan before April 2027.

The department considered a previous modification approved in 2019, and found that a new development application was not needed.

Crucial for the community

According to Idemitsu, the Boggabri coal mine provides about 875 jobs, with most workers living locally.

President of the Boggabri business chamber Suzanne Torrens said the expansion would continue to provide crucial jobs for the area.

"Without the mining industry, our community wouldn't survive," she said.

"It's going to help keep our younger generation in the town as it creates job opportunities."

Suzanne Torrens says the Boggabri mine is the largest employer in the area. (supplied)

Ms Torrens said she understood opponents' concerns but trusted the operator to follow environmental impact standards.

"I believe the mines are doing everything in their ability to make sure the area does go back to its natural state," she said.

Idemitsu declined to comment on the modification approval.

title: Kyrgios free to compete after accepting one-month cocaine ban
text:
Nick Kyrgios has entered a treatment program after accepting a one-month ban for testing positive to cocaine.

After admitting his "huge mistake" when initially suspended for failing a drugs test on June 22 at an ATP 250 tournament in Spain, Kyrgios is allowed to compete again from Friday.

Kyrgios, who had been provisionally suspended since August 4, had faced a ban ranging from a baseline three-month period to up to four years.

During an interview with International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) investigators, Kyrgios explained his use of cocaine had occurred socially during a night out, days before he was due to play in Mallorca.

The ITIA consulted an independent scientific expert at a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory, who stated the explanation was consistent with the level of cocaine found in his sample.

As a result, the ITIA accepted Kyrgios's use of cocaine was outside of competition.

Nick Kyrgios has entered a treatment program. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Under WADA rules, the default suspension for a breach of this type is three months, which can be further reduced to one month if the individual commits to a treatment program approved by the ITIA.

The 2022 Wimbledon finalist also forfeited the 6,570 Euros he won in Mallorca for losing in the first round to countryman Adam Walton.

But his suspension was reduced for agreeing to enter a treatment program.

The ITIA said Kyrgios, whose career world ranking peaked at number 13, could appeal against the provisional suspension, but he opted against doing so.

"I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine," Kyrgios posted on Instagram last month.

"I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it.

"I'm sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I'm sorry to the kids who follow me. I know the example this sets and I'm deeply disappointed in myself."

Kyrgios, who played only four official singles matches on the elite ATP Tour this year, has battled knee and wrist injuries in recent years and has all but conceded he is finished as a singles force.

"I'm not going to make excuses, but I do want to give some context about where I've been," he wrote.

"The last couple of years of injuries have taken a huge toll on me, both physically and mentally.

"My body hasn't been able to do what my mind expects it to do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined."

Nick Kyrgios has been beset by injuries. (AP: Charles Krupa)

But the polarising Canberra-born drawcard said that did not excuse his actions.

"I've always said I didn't choose tennis — tennis chose me," he wrote.

"But letting go of something that has been my whole life is one of the hardest things I've ever had to face. At times I've felt helpless and alone.

"None of that excuses what I did."

Kyrgios said "the good news is that this has given me a wake up call".

"For the next 28 days, I'll be stepping away from social media and public life while I focus on getting myself right.

"I'd ask that people respect my privacy during that time, and most importantly the privacy of my family.

"I'm sorry. I'll do the work and come back better."

The ITIA said Kyrgios was suspended for a ‌positive test for benzoylecgonine, a cocaine metabolite, with a World Anti-Doping Agency laboratory confirming the positive result on July 17.

The 31-year-old was banned from playing, coaching or attending any tournaments sanctioned by the men's and women's tennis tours worldwide and national-level events in Australia.

title: Traditional owners say national park can 'breathe again' after handback
text:
After decades of fighting to reclaim their ancestral land, traditional owners say Boodjamulla National Park can finally "breathe again" now that it is being returned.

About a 4-hour drive north-west of Mount Isa, Boodjamulla is one of outback Queensland's most popular national parks, drawing more than 20,000 visitors each year to sites such as Lawn Hill Gorge and the World Heritage-listed Riversleigh fossil deposits.

Today, more than 247,000 hectares of Boodjamulla will be formally returned to the Waanyi people, who have maintained a connection to the country for more than 30,000 years.

Boodjamulla National Park is about a 4-hour drive north-west of Mount Isa. (supplied: Waanyi PBC)

Hayley Iles, chair of the Waanyi Prescribed Body Corporate (PBC), which represents traditional owners, said the handback felt like "a long-awaited homecoming".

"The land breathes again," Ms Iles said.

"Our elders fought very long to let everyone know that this is our country. This is our land. This is where we do our practices.

"To be sanctioned by the white man to say that's ours, is important … I think there's going to probably be a little bit of crying."

Hayley Iles says Boodjamulla being handed back feels like a "homecoming". (ABC News: Tim Little)

Boodjamulla, meaning rainbow serpent country, is known for its deep gorges and flowing water, which cut through the surrounding plains.

After being dispossessed of their land, generations of Waanyi people endured long and often bitter fights for recognition of their country.

In 1994, Waanyi people and other native title groups staged a three-week sit in at Boodjamulla, demanding greater say in the management of the park and nearby Century Mine.

Lawn Hill Gorge made headlines when it was used in Tourism Australia's Crocodile Dundee ad campaign. (Supplied: Tourism & Events Queensland)

Ms Iles said the protest, followed by another in 2002, helped build momentum.

"Our elders negotiated with people from Carpentaria Land Council, lawyers, anthropologists to get royalty payments out of Century Mine," she said.

"That was the start of it."

Formal negotiations between the Waanyi Native Title Aboriginal Corporation and the Queensland government began in 2020, paving the way for the park's return.

The land was progressively transferred in three stages, with the final tranche completed in January this year.

Boodjamulla was converted from a cattle station to a national park in 1984, before being expanded in 1992. (Supplied: Waanyi PBC)

Department of Tourism, Science and Innovation executive director Karrell Ross said the agreement required the park to be leased back to the state.

"There are other models, but this one is very unique … part of the … [agreement] is funding in perpetuity," Ms Ross said.

"So, there is still a responsibility for the department and still a responsibility for Waanyi PBC.

"We've got a board of management with equal representation … it's about working together."

Boodjamulla National Park has been leased back to the state government to ensure ongoing access for visitors. (Supplied: Qld Department of Environment and Science)

Ms Ross said visitors travelling to the national park should not expect any "huge changes" to access or services.

The significant change was the land was recognised as Aboriginal land, Ms Ross said.

"You'll see both Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service and Waanyi rangers working together, sharing their knowledge, the Waanyi people sharing their cultural knowledge of the area and QPWS also sharing their knowledge about managing land."

Waanyi people have ancestral ties to Boodjamulla dating back more than 30,000 years. (Supplied: Waanyi PBC)

For Ms Iles, today's ceremony represents a triumph following immense work, and a reminder of the time it all took.

"I have family travelling from New South Wales and the Northern Territory … families are coming from all over, so I am jumping out of my skin," she said.

"There is a bit of sadness, because there was a lot of our elders that fought for us to be doing what we're going to be doing [today], who are now gone.

"It is a testament to the resilience, patience and enduring spirit of our elders and our ancestors."

title: Australian battler crushes Italian star in US Open boilover
text:
Dane Sweeny has won a real-life David-versus-Goliath battle to rock the US Open with a stunning second-round upset over dual grand slam semi-finalist Lorenzo Musetti.

The unheralded Australian wildcard took down the 14th seed 3-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-2 on Friday morning (AEST) for the biggest win of his career.

Standing only 170cm high, Sweeny rose to the occasion to reach the third round of a grand slam for the first time and earn a minimum pay day of $US290,000 ($A402,750).

For a couple of heady hours it looked like his underdog countrymen Tristan Schoolkate and Alexei Popyrin would join Sweeny in round three.

Osaka, Keys mount thrilling fightbacks Naomi Osaka wobbled through the second set to fight back and beat Kateřina Siniaková in three, while Madison Keys staved off five match points to keep her US Open dreams alive on day of high drama at Flushing Meadows.

But Schoolkate's inspired run from qualifying finally came to a halt at the hands of fifth-seeded French Open runner-up Flavio Cobilli.

Schoolkate snatched the first set before the Italian showed his class to prevail 3-6, 6-3, 6-4, 7-5 after two hours and 41 minutes in New York's scorching summer heat.

And two years after upstaging Novak Djokovic in the US Open's third round, Popyrin fell short of a place in the last 32 once again, losing a tense four-set battle with Chilean Alejandro Tabilo.

Like Schoolkate, Popyrin took the opening set before the 25th-seeded South American claimed two pivotal tiebreakers, then the match 2-6, 7-6 (7-4), 7-6 (7-3), 6-2 to seal a likely third-round date with German top seed Alexander Zverev.

But ranked more than 100 places below his world number 14 opponent, Sweeny is savouring a mighty breakthrough after bossing Musetti into submission.

He ran the 14th seed ragged and had the Italian looking in particular distress when he required a medical time-out after falling behind a double break at 0-3 in the all-important third set.

Even after clawing one break back, Musetti — who has made the Wimbledon and French Open semi-finals over the past two years — continued remonstrating animatedly to his courtside box.

Despite sporting a massive ice pack on his right elbow after his first-round win, Sweeny continued diving like Boris Becker for acrobatic winning volleys at the net.

And the 25-year-old was duly rewarded with a last-32 shot at another Italian, world number 22 Luciano Darderi on Saturday (AEST) — and a rankings rise to a career-best 115 in the world, or better.

"I'm just grateful to be even able to compete in grand slams. The tennis journey is such a rollercoaster," Sweeny said.

"And to soak up the atmosphere and get a win, a couple of wins, in front of this crowd, is awesome."

title: In Nepal, hope gives way to grief. Few are counting on miracles
text:
Dawa Yangji Tamang is mourning the loss of her son, her daughter-in-law and her grandchildren in the Tibetan flood.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thulo Bharkhu, Nepal: It is the first day of Buddhist mourning in the heartbroken village of Thulo Bharkhu, and a grandmother is weeping by two photos she has fixed to her dresser. They show Santu Tamang, the only one of her six children to attend university, dressed sharply in a blazer, smiling beside his wife, Pasang. In the other frame, Yanin, 3, is sat rugged up against the cold, his little sister, Bhechen, cosied between his legs. On paper, they are missing, but Dawa Yangji Tamang, 66, knows they are dead. Too many days have passed now. Nepalese rescuers sifting the river banks and obliterated villages along the Trishuli River are finding body parts, not survivors. So Dawa lights candles under photos from the family’s recent holiday to the capital of Kathmandu, and cries. “I have lost my will to live,” she says. Dawa Yangji Tamang mourns the loss of her son, her daughter-in-law and her grandchildren. All four were claimed by the flash floods that have devastated areas at the Nepal-Tibet border. Kate Geraghty Thulo Bharkhu village, built onto a mountainside in Nepal’s stunning Himalayas, lost 22 sons and daughters on Wednesday last week when a glacial collapse near the border with Tibet sent an inland tidal wave tearing down the Trishuli River.

Advertisement

The Ghewa ceremony being carried out for bus driver Karma Waleya Tamang, who is believed to have perished while ferrying passengers back from the Tibet border. Kate Geraghty Residents of Thulo Bharkhu, a hamlet that lost 22 people in the floods, pray for their deceased loved ones even as the search continues to recover their bodies. Kate Geraghty The dead had been working out of town along the river corridor, providing for their families. Those families, 12 households in total, are now performing the first of what will be a year-long series of rituals to send their loved ones peacefully to the next life. Ordinarily, the bodies would have been cremated soon after death. Families mourn their own, then go up the street to help other families mourn theirs. No one is talking about miracles. The rituals mark an acceptance, and they are accepting together. They serve calorific cups of a local tea made with salt, wildflower and yak butter. In Tamang culture, when people eat at funeral rituals, called Ghewa, they are also eating for the dead. The families, ever warm, insist everyone, including this masthead, eats and drinks their fill. Dawa’s son Santu, an engineer, was the pride of the family. For a time, he had even worked in Japan. When a job came up at the Rasuwagadhi hydro plant, one of many stations harnessing Nepal’s snow-fed rivers, he moved his family there. Santu’s relatives believe he died at work. Pasang and the children would have been taken at home.

Advertisement

Dawa was on a video call with the kids only the day before. They were chirping “amma”, she says – the Nepali word for grandmother With luck, she will get their bodies. Nepal has called for international help with processing DNA and testing. For now, marked body bags are being buried in mass graves in Chitwan district. Some are going in ambulances and police buses. Anyone caught within a dozen vehicles behind will know because of the smell. Hundreds of bodies and parts have washed all the way into India. The ones recovered in Nepal are coming out of ruins or being picked out of the muddy banks. It’s possible thousands are buried under the freshly laid quicksand. Nepalese police carry bodies to a helicopter for a flight to Chitwan, where hundreds of disaster victims are being buried. Kate Geraghty A woman among destroyed buildings in Betrawoti, which was severely affected by the Nepal flash flood that has killed more than a thousand people. Thousands are still missing. Kate Geraghty The market town of Betrawoti has been swallowed up by a deluge of mud. Many of its buildings have been destroyed. Kate Geraghty Only at river level can you appreciate the volume of water the people were up against. Steep mountainsides at the narrow passes are sheared clean of any vegetation 50 metres above the present river level.

Advertisement

It will grow back. Bridges will be rebuilt, eventually. But the damage to villages such as Thulo Bharkhu will last. The pain extends beyond borders and ocean, linking this small, unknown village with a profound grief being felt on many shores. At the most recent count, 36 Australians are feared dead. Mendo Lapachi, who lost her brother and two sisters-in-law, reacts to talking of her family and the flood as she gets ready to hold the Ghewa ceremony. Kate Geraghty Destroyed buildings in Betrawoti. Kate Geraghty Chogyal Dorje Lama is holding a Ghewa for his wife, Pratima, his brother Thile and sister-in-law Chenku. All three were killed in Syabrubesi, about a kilometre away on the banks of the Trishuli. Chogyal’s wife, the deputy mayor, managed one final call to her husband as the river bore down. “She was saying, ‘My mother, my mother, mother,’” he says. It is Nepalese equivalent of “my god”. Chogyal says it sounded like she was running. “Then the voice was gone,” he says. “That voice is still coming to my head. How can I forget?” He gazes mournfully at Pratima’s framed portrait resting low on a coffee table, recalling the community work she did for children and the elderly, how she was made to run for deputy mayor by insistent locals.

Advertisement

The couple were just about to try for a family. “Now, I am alone. So how to live?” Chogyal asks. Chogyal Dorje Lama sits near photos of his wife, Pratima Tamang (right), who was a nurse and deputy mayor of the local council and was in an office building in Syabrubesi when the floods hit. Kate Geraghty Syabrubesi is best known as the starting point of the Langtang Valley trek. It is also a stopover for Hindu pilgrims on their way north to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash. Chogyal’s brother owned one of Syabrubesi’s hotels, the Royal Himalayan, and was probably inside with Chenku and guests as it was swept away at about 9am. The hotel was fully booked with 70 to 80 people the night before the flood, Chogyal believes. At least four of the guests were Australians. Sydney’s Sreedharan Iyer, 53, his wife, Lakshmi, 49, and the couple’s two sons, Rishab, 23, and Rudhra, 20, were travelling as part of a group of 15 Australian pilgrims, most of whom stayed the night before the tragedy at the Hotel Kailash, close to the border. That hotel was swept away, too. The pilgrims are part of a wider group of Australians caught up in the tragedy.

SportTennisUS Open De Minaur dumped from US Open in straight sets as Kyrgios cocaine ban revealed Marc McGowan Updated September 4, 2026 — 1:41pm ,first published September 4, 2026 — 8:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Alex de Minaur could relinquish his top-10 ranking within weeks after a second-round US Open defeat capped his least-successful grand slam season in three years. The world No.7 suffered a 6-4, 7-5, 6-2 loss to dangerous Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp in New York on Friday (AEST), continuing a prolonged form downturn after a brilliant start to his 2026 campaign. Loading De Minaur’s disappointing exit came on a dramatic day at Flushing Meadows, where wildcard Dane Sweeny was the sole Australian to progress to the round of 32 after toppling fancied Italian Lorenzo Musetti. It also happened as Nick Kyrgios accepted a one-month suspension for out-of-competition use of cocaine.

Advertisement

“My level today wasn’t good enough. It’s pretty straightforward,” de Minaur said. “I gave myself every chance by being competitive, having a good mindset, a good attitude, but it was just one of those days when the feeling of the ball on the strings wasn’t there. De Minaur stretches for a forehand. AP Photo/Frank Franklin II “I was making a lot of errors, which is not really my normal game style. I can’t really explain the reasoning of it, but it felt like the more I tried, the more intensity, the more fired up I was getting, I just kept on making unforced errors … [it was] a tough day at the office.” De Minaur lost this early in a major only twice in his past 13 events.

Advertisement

He advanced to a second Australian Open quarter-final in January, but bowed out in the third and fourth rounds at Roland-Garros and Wimbledon, respectively. De Minaur reached the US Open quarter-finals the past two years, and his defeat – his earliest in New York in five years – means wildcard Sweeny is the only Australian still in singles contention. Alex de Minaur suffered a disappointing second-round loss at the US Open. Getty Images Sweeny, a 170-centimetre battler ranked 123 in the world, is celebrating his maiden top-20 victory, taking down Italy’s dual grand slam semi-finalist Musetti 3-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-2 in a titanic upset to reach the third round for the first time. It is van de Zandschulp’s second major scalp at the US Open after eliminating Carlos Alcaraz in the same round two years ago, but he had never beaten de Minaur in four prior meetings.

Advertisement

The result was an upset on paper only, given power-hitting van de Zandschulp entered the tournament in better form than de Minaur, who has made it beyond the quarter-finals at any event only once since February. The 27-year-old was crestfallen after his Wimbledon defeat to Flavio Cobolli in July, saying afterwards that not stepping up on that stage “breaks me inside”. He played down his devastated post-match reaction in Washington a few weeks later, but has struggled on court since. Australia’s Dane Sweeny is breaking new ground at this year’s US Open. AP Photo/Seth Wenig De Minaur’s much-scrutinised serve failed him against van de Zandschulp, committing seven double faults compared to only four aces, while conceding 11 break points and dropping serve five times. He hit one of those double faults to go a set and 4-3 down, but a stroke of fortune in the next game could have proven a turning point. After some fabulous defence, a de Minaur backhand clipped the net cord and whizzed past van de Zandschulp for a winner to reduce him to 15-40.

Advertisement

De Minaur drew level, then edged ahead, but lost a marathon service game at 5-5 after saving four break points before conceding on the fifth. Van de Zandschulp apologised because a mishit ball landed short in the court to drag de Minaur into the net and create his forehand pass opportunity, but the Australian could have done more. The Dutchman went two sets up, and the odds were against de Minaur, who had never erased that deficit in 27 attempts. After going off court between sets, de Minaur tried to up the ante, but flayed a forehand long in the third game to drop serve. Two break-back points came and went in the next game before van de Zandschulp broke his top-10 rival once more to as good as seal the Aussie’s fate. Little has happened easily for Sweeny in his until-now off-Broadway tennis career, so he was due some good fortune – and it is coming in spades at this US Open.

Advertisement

Musetti spent most of the final three sets physically struggling, hunched over in the corner of the court and generally looking under the weather. He took an off-court medical timeout after going 3-0 down in the third set, and showed the odd sign of life, but Sweeny never let up. Sweeny’s only previous match against this calibre of opponent was a straight-sets defeat to American star Ben Shelton in the second round at this year’s Australian Open. He is now guaranteed a payday of more than $400,000, and is provisionally at a career-high live ranking of No.109 ahead of another on-court date with a seeded Italian, Luciano Darderi. “I’m so grateful to be able to even compete in grand slams,” Sweeny said. Loading

Advertisement

“I put a lot of work in. The tennis journey is such a rollercoaster, and I’m so incredibly grateful to play in front of an awesome crowd and to soak up this moment. To win, and to get a couple of wins, is awesome.” This milestone moment comes barely two years since Sweeny took a multi-month break from the sport after suffering through a form slump, just as he felt close to finally breaking through into elite company. “That’s the beautiful thing about pursuing something so hard like tennis,” he said. “Tennis can change on the flip of a coin. You’ve just got to keep persevering, and that’s what I did. I wasn’t getting results for a long while, but there’s a law of probability. I knew it was somehow going to swing in my favour if I just kept going, and I did. “Now I’m here, and it’s the best decision I ever made to come back after that two months.”

Advertisement

Australia’s Nick Kyrgios served a one-month ban for using cocaine. AP Meanwhile, the International Tennis Integrity Agency announced on Friday morning that Kyrgios had accepted a one-month suspension for out-of-competition use of cocaine, while agreeing to enter a treatment program that reduces the ban from three months. Kyrgios apologised to his family, friends and fans last month for making a “huge mistake” when his provisional suspension was revealed. He admitted to the ITIA that he used cocaine socially on a night out before he competed in Mallorca. Kyrgios’ suspension officially ended on Thursday, subject to him completing his treatment program, and he forfeited his prizemoney and ranking points from the Mallorca event. Former doubles partner Stefanos Tsitsipas, whom Kyrgios has feuded with, said after his first-round US Open victory that the news did not surprise him and that he was aware of the situation.

Alexei Popyrin is out of the US Open in the second round. AP Photo/Andres Kudacki For a while, a second Australian underdog seemed poised to upset a highly ranked Italian as qualifier Tristan Schoolkate snatched the first set from Roland-Garros finalist Cobolli, only to go down 3-6, 6-3, 6-4, 7-5 to the No.5 seed. A dispirited Alexei Popyrin also exited the US Open, losing 2-6, 7-6 (7-4), 7-6 (7-3), 6-2 to 25th-seeded Chilean left-hander Alejandro Tabilo after a bright start. The Musetti result continued some overdue luck for Sweeny, who was supposed to contest US Open qualifying, but several player withdrawals enabled Popyrin to make the main draw cut-off, and transferred Tennis Australia’s reciprocal wildcard to him. The 25-year-old parlayed his wildcard into his first grand slam win outside Melbourne Park when Frenchman Corentin Moutet retired with an arm injury while trailing 7-6 (7-4), 6-4, 3-0.

It’s never been that simple Marc McGowan Sports reporter Musetti was dressed head-to-toe in sponsored Asics gear, whereas the mustachioed Sweeny wore a plain white shirt and red cap to shade him from the harsh and humid New York heat. The war wounds on Sweeny’s elbows and knees were evidence of his scrappy style, too. Everything changed after a relatively routine opening set, albeit one Sweeny had chances in. Musetti began looking off-colour during the second set, which he lost in lopsided fashion, and never fully recovered despite glimpses of his usual spectacular shot-making. Like the second set, Musetti quickly handed over a pair of breaks in the third.

He twice recovered a break, only to hand it straight back to Sweeny, whose relentless hitting and scampering never wavered. The fourth set took a similar path as Musetti gifted an immediate break of serve that left him playing catch up again. A spokesman for the labour group also said that compulsory layoffs at Volkswagen remain ruled out through the end of 2030 under existing agreements.

That distinction reflects the broader compromise behind the unanimous board vote, reached a day earlier than initially expected after weeks of increasingly bitter rhetoric. Labour representatives had accepted that Volkswagen needed further cost reductions. But they fiercely opposed plant closures, moves to weaken co-determination – Germany’s system of worker representation in corporate decisions – and plans to separate parts of the core VW business. VW’s US depositary receipts jumped about 9 per cent in New York on Thursday, the most since March 2023. Chief executive officer Oliver Blume has been given his clearest mandate yet to remake Europe’s biggest carmaker. Bloomberg In the final package, Blume won backing for the extra job cuts and sweeping efficiency measures. Workers secured assurances that no factory would be immediately abandoned and that contentious site decisions would instead be worked through over the coming months. The agreement gives the CEO stronger backing to push ahead as VW struggles with high costs, weak demand and intensifying competition, particularly from Chinese carmakers. The deal stops short of immediately closing factories. VW acknowledged that it currently has about 500,000 vehicles-worth of excess annual capacity in Europe. The company said its factories in Emden, Hannover, Neckarsulm and Zwickau currently lack competitive future production plans once existing models phase out between 2031 and 2034. Alternative uses for the plants will now be explored, Volkswagen said.

Advertisement

That gave labour-friendly board members room to support the overhaul without abandoning core red lines. IG Metall chief Christiane Benner and works council head Daniela Cavallo said the compromise had “prevented a dangerous escalation”, while stressing that no plant closing had been agreed upon and that plans to separate the VW passenger-car and components businesses were off the table. “The work is only just beginning,” the labour chiefs said of the restructuring plan. “What we will continue never to accept, however, is the burden being placed one-sidedly on employees.” Benner said the carmaker was dealing with a “crisis situation”. Tablets may be the answer The Porsche-Piëch family, which controls a majority of VW’s voting rights through Porsche SE, has pushed for faster action as returns and dividend flows come under pressure. Blume has argued that Volkswagen can no longer afford to carry the same sprawling cost base and industrial footprint while funding investments in electric vehicles, batteries and software. Porsche SE “welcomes this decision and intends to continue to support the transformation efforts of the board of management of its core investment, Volkswagen AG,” a spokesperson for Porsche SE said in a statement.

The overhaul targets an operating margin of 9 per cent by 2030 on annual sales of about 9 million vehicles. VW is also planning €135 billion of capital expenditure and research and development spending over 2027 through 2031, the company said. title: An $1080 share investment I made in 1993 is now worth $204,000. Should I sell?
text:
I have about 1300 Commbank shares. l started off with 200 in 1993 and have just kept going with the dividend reinvestment plan. With the tax changes coming in July 2027, should l be selling them before that date? I am 65, my wife is 66,and we plan to retire at about that time. We have no debt and a reasonable sum in each of our super funds.

That $1080 investment you made back in 1993 is now worth $204,000. Simon Letch

The most important ingredient to investment and wealth creation success is patience, something most of us struggle with. So firstly, a big “well done” for sitting on these shares for more than 30 years. That $1080 investment you made back in 1993 is now worth $204,000, a fantastic outcome, and a great illustration of the wisdom of investing into productive businesses via shares.

There are several reasons why you might choose to sell these shares – to boost your super on retirement, to help a family member, to buy a caravan and hit the road, and I’m sure there is plenty more. But selling them because of the tax changes coming in 2027 is not one of them.

From July next year the way capital gains tax is calculated will change. But that change only affects the period from 1 July 2027 onwards. It has no impact on your tax treatment up to that point. This change is therefore in no way a catalyst to induce a sale that you otherwise would not have made.

title: This $800 Dyson toothbrush is selling out. But is it really worth the hype?
text:

LifestyleHealth & wellnessOral health This $800 Dyson toothbrush is selling out. But is it really worth the hype? Shona Hendley September 4, 2026 — 12:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Have you ever wanted to see what your dentist sees? While many of us would probably answer no, a product that allows you to do just that – the Dyson CameraJet electric toothbrush – has hit the market. And it’s causing quite the buzz. Dyson’s foray into oral care, touted as the “complete oral care routine in one toothbrush”, includes an array of functions, including jet washing, liquid flossing and mouthwash dispensing. Retailing at $799, the Dyson CameraJet electric toothbrush can show you things you’ve never seen before (and may never want to see again). But along with the hefty $799 price tag, it’s the integrated 100k-pixel macro-lens camera that is attracting the most attention. This feature, which Dyson says can detect, track and predict gaps between teeth in real time, is also said to remove “up to 72 per cent more plaque than market-leading electric toothbrushes” by delivering a targeted jet of mouthwash to the detected area.

Advertisement

This mouthwash, along with toothpaste, needs to be non- or low-foaming, so the camera can see clearly. The brand has launched its own line of these products, retailing at $15.99 each. Dyson says these features – including an app which gives you feedback on your brushing, after analysing footage – set the CameraJet apart. But are people willing to fork out almost $800 on a toothbrush and, most importantly, what do dentists think? Do people really want it? From the brand that has generated cult followings for many of its products, from cordless vacuums to the Dyson Airwrap, you’d assume this could follow suit. At the time of publishing, the CameraJet is out of stock on the Dyson Australia website but available from other retailers, including JB Hi-Fi, The Good Guys and Harvey Norman. However, exact sales figures in Australia remain unconfirmed.

Advertisement

Related Article Wellness Is your beloved sparkling water damaging your teeth? “Dyson does not comment on specific sales performance. But we’re delighted by the initial response and engagement we’ve seen from consumers so far,” says Niamh Turney, a senior engineer and commercial manager at Dyson. On social media, led by influencers, gadget reviewers and users from the dental industry, #dysontoothbrush has accumulated over 600,000 posts on TikTok, while Instagram has seen mixed reactions, including jokes about the live-stream feature and outrage over the product’s cost. What do dentists think? Dr Monica Farrelly, a dentist and Oral Health Promoter for the Australian Dental Association, says much of the hype is likely attributable to the brand rather than the product itself.

Advertisement

“Dyson entering a completely new category always draws coverage,” she says, adding that the “novelty factor” of a toothbrush with a camera and the product’s price point may also have contributed. Feature-wise, Farrelly believes it is too early to say with confidence whether the product deserves the attention or the price tag. The product’s conical jet is said to be more effective and gentler on gums than other water flossers. “Independent, peer-reviewed clinical research on the CameraJet specifically doesn’t exist yet, since the product has only just launched,” she says. However, she says that “the underlying idea – a toothbrush that helps people clean interdental gaps more consistently – is genuinely useful because interdental cleaning is where most people fall short.”

Advertisement

“Whether the camera and AI targeting deliver meaningfully better results than a person using a water flosser or interdental brushes properly is not yet established,” she adds. Editor's pick Fertility Single at 30, Chloe decided to freeze her eggs. She wasn’t prepared for what came next She also has some reservations about the camera being used by people without dental training. “It may be difficult for people to know what they are looking at: is it plaque, calculus or a hole?” Farrelly says. “The camera itself also only shows you limited surfaces of the teeth. Even as dentists, we need to take X-rays to accurately detect all things in the mouth.” Dr Giulia D’Anna, principal dentist at iDental, says most of the features of the product that look good are the usual features of an electric toothbrush.

Advertisement

“A small round oscillating head is good at being able to target small spaces well, with minimal movement required from the user,” she says. “This means hard-to-reach areas are better brushed.” What to look for in a toothbrush When looking for and choosing an electric toothbrush, D’Anna says that in addition to the small head size, she recommends: A pressure sensor that alerts when you’re brushing too hard

A 30-second timer function. She recommends 30 seconds of brushing for the lower outside, lower inside, upper inner and upper outer segments – so two minutes total “These features are generally included in a brush that retails for around $120 to $180,” D’Anna explains.

Advertisement

Farrelly says that individual factors – age, orthodontic appliances such as braces, gum conditions such as recession – should be considered when choosing an electric or non-electric toothbrush, as people with sensitive teeth or gums benefit from soft bristles or a gentle brushing mode if using an electric brush. According to Farrelly, manual brushes are often perfectly adequate, though older adults or people with reduced hand dexterity often do best with an electric toothbrush with large, easy-to-grip handles. title: 'Beneath their office': Why the US-Canada dispute has turned so nasty
text:
IN BRIEF Trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed last month after Canada rejected what it called unacceptable US demands.

Donald Trump has escalated the dispute with tariffs, personal attacks and repeated suggestions Canada should become a US state.

What began as a trade fight between two of the world's most closely connected economies has escalated into a broader confrontation over Canada's sovereignty, culture and military, with United States President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney now trading increasingly personal attacks.

The latest escalation follows the collapse of trade talks between the two countries on 21 August.

Canada walked away from negotiations after saying the US had made unacceptable last-minute demands, while the US has argued there was a deal on the table that Canada chose not to accept.

The US has since imposed 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars of Canadian goods, with Canada preparing retaliatory measures of its own.

Since then, the dispute has spilled well beyond trade. Trump has repeatedly suggested Canada should become the 51st US state, ordered US federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario as "Lake America" and continued to attack Canadian leaders online.

US officials have also mocked Canada's military, prompting Carney to accuse Washington of "doing memes", "throwing shade" and "trying to be tough".

But beneath the memes and insults is a serious economic standoff that both sides still say could ultimately be resolved at the negotiating table.

Origins of the feud

While Trump has imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about US$20 billion ($27 billion) worth of Canadian goods, Canada is preparing retaliatory tariffs of roughly the same value on US products from 8 September.

But the disagreement isn't just about tariffs.

Carney says the US was seeking terms that would have left major Canadian industries, particularly the highly integrated auto sector, effectively operating as subsidiaries of US companies.

He has also accused the US of seeking changes that would affect Canada's French-language and cultural protections, as well as restrictions on Canada's ability to negotiate future free trade agreements with other countries.

Canada has rejected those demands as a threat to its economic interests and sovereignty.

The Trump administration disputes Canada's account of the negotiations and has argued that a deal was available that Canada chose not to accept.

Why has sovereignty become such a big issue?

Trump has repeatedly suggested that Canada should become the 51st US state, a proposal Canada has firmly rejected.

What might once have sounded like political provocation has become a central part of the dispute, with Carney increasingly framing the confrontation as a defence of Canadian sovereignty.

That rhetoric carries particular weight in Quebec, where there are concerns about what US absorption of Canada could mean for the province's French language and culture.

Carney has also pushed back against any suggestion that the US should have a say over who Canada trades with.

"Canada is a sovereign state," he said.

"We will strike free trade deals with the countries we wish to strike free trade deals with."

Why is the rhetoric getting so personal?

Since the trade talks collapsed, Trump has repeatedly attacked Canada's leadership and used social media to taunt the country.

He has described Canada's leaders as among the worst he has to deal with, and posted an AI-generated meme depicting Canadian geese with his distinctive hairstyle marching under a US flag.

US defence secretary Pete Hegseth appeared to take aim at Canada's military, posting an image of two female Canadian military cadets training in British Columbia with the words "this is real" alongside a Canadian flag.

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent also mocked Canada's military, later saying that Carney had received a "verbal beatdown" from him and Hegseth.

Carney said the comments from members of Trump's administration were "beneath their office".

"When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions," Carney said.

Why does it matter beyond the insults?

The US and Canada have one of the world's most deeply integrated economic relationships.

That means prolonged disruption could affect workers, businesses and consumers on both sides of the border, particularly in industries such as manufacturing and autos, where supply chains frequently cross the border.

The Canadian government has warned that it cannot accept an agreement that it believes would weaken its domestic industries or limit its ability to make its own economic decisions.

At the same time, Carney has stressed that Canada is not looking for a permanent economic rupture with its largest trading partner.

On Thursday, he said Canada was ready to sign a deal with the US if it benefited both countries and provided "stability and credibility".

He also suggested there had been a recent softening in Washington's position.

Carney said the US had been pushing certain demands around Canadian language and culture right up until the talks collapsed, but was no longer insisting on them.

"Now, they're not," he said. "Well, if they didn't care, they shouldn't have kept them in the deal."

Is a deal still possible?

Despite the increasingly bitter rhetoric, Carney says the door to negotiations remains open.

He has repeatedly said Canada is prepared to return to the table when the US is ready to have serious discussions.

Trump's response has been less conciliatory.

After Carney's comments on Thursday, Trump posted that it was "very good for Canadian Politicians like Prime Minister Mark Carney to make President Donald J. Trump 'the enemy.'"

He warned that Canada's economy could collapse and be "worse than anything that has ever happened to a Canadian politician".

So while the memes, insults and threats have grabbed the headlines, the underlying dispute remains fundamentally about power.

Canada is trying to protect its industries and preserve its ability to make independent economic and cultural decisions.

Trump's administration is pushing for a trade relationship on terms more favourable to the US.

And both sides are now testing how far they are willing to go, without completely severing a relationship that neither country can easily walk away from.

title: Argentine president reignites Falklands dispute after Trump questions UK sovereignty
text:
In brief Argentine President Javier Milei has reignited a dispute with the United Kingdom over the Falkland Islands.

It comes after US President Donald Trump said the US would reconsider its neutral stance on the islands' sovereignty.

Argentine President Javier Milei escalated his country's long-running dispute with the United Kingdom over the Falkland Islands, praising US President Donald Trump for saying the US could reconsider its historically neutral stance on the islands' sovereignty.

In a nationally televised address on Thursday night local time, Milei seized on Trump's comments this week that the US could review its position on the islands, casting the potential shift as proof that his close relationship with the US president — often criticised by political opponents — was paying dividends.

"The United States is considering this change in position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with Western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come," Milei said.

The libertarian Argentine leader then announced a series of actions aimed at stopping the development of the Sea Lion oil project, about 220km north of the islands, where UK company Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum plan to begin drilling in the coming months and start producing oil in 2028.

Argentina considers the project an illegal exploitation of resources in waters it claims as its own.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He threatened tougher sanctions against companies involved in offshore drilling and announced new funding for a naval base in Argentina's southernmost province, Tierra del Fuego, to bolster the country's military presence near the islands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas.

READ MORE Argentina faces FIFA fine after players celebrate win against England with Falklands banner

"Argentina will not stand idly by," Milei said. "Any further advance on the Malvinas Islands will be considered a violation of our national security."

Milei's effort to refocus national attention on the Falklands marks a striking turn for a leader who has faced criticism at home for warming ties with the UK and professing admiration for Margaret Thatcher, the UK prime minister who led the country to retake the remote archipelago during the 1982 Falklands War after Argentina had invaded it.

The two-month conflict killed 649 Argentine troops, 255 British service members and three islanders.

The sovereignty claim remains one of the few causes that cuts across Argentina's stark political divides, giving Milei a welcome political opening as his approval ratings slip and the economy sputters.

"We can argue about my style. We can disagree over fiscal or exchange-rate policy," Milei said.

"But this issue demands that we lay down our arms and show a united front to the world as a nation and as a society. There are causes that rise above any political difference. The Malvinas is one of them."

Argentina maintains that it inherited sovereignty over the islands from its former coloniser, Spain, and that the UK has illegally occupied them since 1833. The UK rejects that claim, citing the islanders' desire to remain a British overseas territory.

Trump questions US support for British sovereignty

For decades, successive US administrations have remained neutral on the competing Argentine and UK sovereignty claims over the Falklands while recognising the UK's de facto administration of the islands. Any departure from that position would be a major diplomatic affront and inflame already high trans-Atlantic tensions.

On Monday, Trump fuelled frenzied speculation in the UK when asked whether his administration was reviewing its stance on the decades-old dispute.

"I always review every position," he replied. "That's just one of many."

Then, in an interview aired on Thursday with UK broadcaster GB News, Trump avoided directly answering a question about whether the US would "come to the aid" of the UK in another conflict over the Falklands.

The Falkland Islands have been under UK control for nearly 200 years. Credit: Supplied

Instead, he repeated past complaints that Britain had not provided sufficient support for the US-led bombing campaign against Iran.

"Your country was not there to help me," Trump said, recalling that the UK's former prime minister, Keir Starmer, told him the country did not have ships to contribute to the campaign.

"It was pretty sad, the whole thing."

The Trump administration has floated the Falklands as leverage before: An internal Pentagon email leaked in April first raised the prospect of the US reconsidering its position on the islands as one possible way to punish NATO allies that declined to join the US war on Iran.

In response, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's spokesman, Tom Wells, said the British government's position was "long-standing and unwavering".

"Sovereignty rests with the UK, and the islanders' right to self-determination is paramount," Wells said earlier this week, pointing to a 2013 referendum in which the roughly 4,000 people living in the Falkland Islands voted overwhelmingly in favour of remaining a British overseas territory.
