title: Feminist icon Gloria Steinem remembered as a 'fearless trailblazer' after death at 92
text:
In brief US feminist icon Gloria Steinem has died at the age of 92.

Tributes have poured in from around the world, with Nancy Pelosi describing her as a "fearless trailblazer".

Tributes have poured in after Gloria Steinem, the United States journalist, author and activist who was one of the most recognisable and enduring faces of the feminist movement, died at age 92.

In a statement on Thursday, Steinem's foundation announced: "Yesterday, Gloria Steinem passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her."

Her death has sparked tributes to her decades of boundary-pushing activism.

Hillary Clinton, the first woman to serve as US secretary of state and the first female US presidential nominee of a major political party, said Steinem "pushed open doors not just for herself, but for literally millions of women behind her".

Nancy Pelosi, the first woman to be US House speaker, called Steinem "a fearless trailblazer who transformed the fight for equality in America and inspired generations of women to know their power".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"She lit a torch many years ago. It is now our responsibility to keep it lifted into the future," tennis champion Billie Jean King, winner of the famed 1973 "Battle of the Sexes" match, said.

Before becoming a leading figure in the women's rights movement, Steinem cut her teeth in journalism in the 1960s, denouncing the inequalities women in the US endured at a time when many needed their husband's approval to open a bank account.

She came to prominence in 1963 with an exposé of the pervasive sexism faced by cocktail waitresses at New York's Playboy Club.

But she credited her awakening to activism to a 1969 meeting where women described the ordeal of having an abortion.

"It made some sense of my own experience. I had had an abortion and had never told anyone," she later recounted in an article in New York Magazine.

The London doctor who gave her an abortion in 1957, when it was still illegal, made her promise two things: "First, you will not tell anyone my name. Second, you will do what you want to do with your life."

In the 1970s, she founded Ms Magazine and the National Women's Political Caucus and organised the first National Women's Conference in Houston.

Gloria Steinem rose to prominence in the 1960s with an exposé on the sexism faced by cocktail waitresses at New York's Playboy Club. Source: Getty / Bettye Lane / Photo Researchers History

Donning her trademark aviator glasses, Steinem headlined conferences and protests in the US and around the world for decades. She remained an outspoken defender of women's rights well into her later years.

When in 2022 the US Supreme Court overturned the Roe v Wade decision of 1973, which had enshrined the right to abortion, she pointed out: "Banning abortions does not stop the need for them. It just bans their safety.

"Don't agonise. Organise," she urged.

After a lifetime battling injustice, she told Agence France-Presse in 2019: "I think the role of older people like me is to have hope, because we remember when it was worse."

Public scrutiny

Born in Ohio on 25 March 1934, Steinem had a nomadic childhood with a travelling salesman father.

Her parents divorced when she was 10, forcing her to care for her mother, who had mental health issues.

As a frontline feminist, she came under intense scrutiny from both sides of the political spectrum.

Her good looks, miniskirts and brief experience as a Playboy Bunny were used against her in attempts to undermine her credibility.

READ MORE Julia Gillard says 'manosphere' requires new approach to gender equality

The fact that she remained single and childless was also weaponised.

At 66, she married businessman David Bale, the father of actor Christian Bale.

Asked by a reporter why she had changed her position on single life, she said: "I didn't change. Marriage changed."

Bale died three years later of brain cancer, aged 62. Steinem herself underwent surgery for breast cancer in the 1980s.

Second-wave feminist leader

Some younger activists saw Steinem — a leader of second-wave feminism from the 1960s to 1980s, which challenged job discrimination, reproductive rights and cultural sexism — as representing an outdated type of feminism.

She was criticised for defending Bill Clinton in 1989 when the then-governor of Arkansas was accused of sexual harassment.

In 2016, when Clinton's wife, Hillary, was vying to become the first female president in US history but struggling to garner support among women, Steinem suggested that young women preferred her rival, Bernie Sanders, because young men liked him.

"When you're young, you're thinking: 'Where are the boys? The boys are with Bernie,'" she told talk show host Bill Maher. She later apologised.

Steinem was given numerous awards and honours, including the US Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013.

Supporters stopped outside Steinem's Manhattan apartment on Thursday to pay respects.

"I'm just feeling very inspired and grateful for the life that she led," Makenna Lorange, 31, who was visiting from Boston, said.

"We've lost a little bit of light in the world... [I'm] feeling renewed inspiration to carry on the torch in my own small ways going forward."

title: Pacific leaders voice concern over Chinese missile test but stop short of condemnation
text:
In brief The Pacific Islands Forum has agreed to "register concern" over a Chinese missile test in July.

The statement falls short of condemnation, and Nauru dissented the clause.

The Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) has wrapped up with most nations agreeing to "register concern" on China's recent intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) test, "which overflew a number of members without adequate notice".

"Leaders call on all states undertaking ICBM testing to ensure transparency and reassurance, including through the provision of advance notification of a test at least 24 hours in accordance with international practice," the communique says, as read out by Palau's President and PIF chair Surangel Whipps Junior, after the closing ceremony.

But it was not unanimous.

In a rare move for the usually consensus-based forum, Nauru was the only one of 18 PIF members to dissent from the clause.

Kiribati and Nauru were the only two Pacific nations that had previously blocked a draft PIF statement in the immediate aftermath of Beijing's test, a move that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had been advocating for.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

However the statement went further than analysts and government sources had expected; the PIF foreign ministers' meeting statement in August was broader, discussing ballistic missile testing in the region, but had stopped short of singling out a particular ICBM or referencing a notice period for nations to undergo any testing.

Whipps also hit back against China's comments that Palau sensationalised its ballistic missile test, saying: "There's no sensationalism, it's just stating the facts."

"The Pacific Islands weren't informed [of the test]. The ones that were informed were informed late, and so I think the message from the forum is clear: that transparency needs to happen."

Intelligence shows the nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missile test in July flew over the Philippines, Palau and Micronesia's airspace before landing in the Pacific Ocean.

Several nations had criticised the test, just the second since 1980.

The response has become something of a litmus test for PIF and its members for their strategic positioning.

READ MORE Albanese responds after China warns of 'consequences' over Taiwan at Pacific summit

The communique's relevant clause includes a reference to the Fiji-led Ocean of Peace declaration made last year, which states the region should be free from coercion and militarisation.

However, it doesn't name China, nor does it use heftier diplomatic language than "concern".

While Australian officials were happy with the agreed statement, it fell short of some pre-retreat expectations, including those of the host, Palau.

Whipps made his displeasure with the test clear, which followed a 2024 effort.

"They sent a missile next to French Polynesia, another one next to Tuvalu, crossing over our airspace. They never bothered to tell us that's what's happening," he said.

"I said 'there's a lot of space between Japan and Guam, why don't you send it there? Why does it have to come to the middle of the Pacific when last year we just signed a declaration of peace?'

"We don't want our backyard, our homes, to be threatened and really disrespected."

Whipps said "a unified Pacific voice" would be critical to get Beijing to "respect sovereignty".

No region-wide pact

In other decisions of the leaders' retreat, PIF will categorise external powers, currently known as "dialogue partners", as either strategic or sector partners.

The 13 strategic partners will be China, the US, France, Germany, the UK, the EU, Canada, Japan, India, Indonesia, Singapore, South Korea and the UAE.

Those partners will be able to continue to travel to leaders' meetings, while sector partners will be referred to the annual foreign ministers gathering.

A region-wide security pact, championed by Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale, did not progress — as expected, given Wale's absence.

A proposal to bring the Australia-backed Joint Heads of Pacific Security under the Pacific Islands Forum has also garnered some support.

title: 'Hard to continue': Harvey's future is in limbo as his sport faces an existential threat
text:
Ski resorts across Australia have faced one of the hottest winters on record. For Australian snowboarder Harvey Edmanson, this is a threat to his future, and to the future of young snow athletes across Australia.

Speaking to SBS, the member of the Australian Alpine Snowboard National Team said: "If I don't have snow and training opportunities in Australia, it's going to make it really hard to continue."

Many professional snow athletes, including Edmanson, are self-funded. He has to fit his training around working as a façade designer in Melbourne.

The 27-year-old does most of his training at Mount Buller in Victoria but also ventures further north to the Perisher and Thredbo resorts in NSW.

Typically, he aims to train on the slopes from early July until late September. This year his start was delayed by three weeks and he was forced to stop in late August.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"It makes it hard when I miss out on over a month of training," Edmanson said.

Additionally, to train at a high level, Edmanson and other athletes need a sectioned-off part of the slope where they can set up racing conditions.

READ MORE Australia’s winter wonderland is becoming increasingly reliant on a backup plan

Ski resorts are usually happy to accommodate this, but have found it harder this year due to having a smaller area with sufficient snow depth.

"When there's only limited snow and limited run hill space, then it's not possible," Edmanson said.

Australian snow athletes often compete overseas during the northern hemisphere’s winter before returning to train in Australia in the off-season.

As snow seasons get shorter, Edmanson said athletes are skipping Australia entirely and starting to look overseas for off-season training.

This is not something he can do given he needs to work, and he joked that he "can't commute to New Zealand".

Mount Buller is a popular snow sports destination north-east of Melbourne. Source: LightRocket / Ye Myo Khant

Will young athletes feel the consequences?

Some in the snow sports community fear for future generations of Australian snow athletes if opportunities continue to dwindle for younger athletes seeking to develop.

Edmanson runs a futures program for developing athletes and says there's a lot of young athletes who are "looking to compete, looking to train, and they don't get enough time on snow in Australia".

Many younger athletes need to balance school and practice. Edmanson didn’t travel overseas to compete until he finished school.

"The most important part of my training and development all happened in Australia," he said. "It's really scary that there's a lot of young athletes that might not have that opportunity."

This year’s Milano Cortina Winter Olympics provided an injection of optimism into Australian snow sports after the Australian team won a national best three golds, two silvers and one bronze.

To continue this momentum, Edmanson says we need to give young athletes "that opportunity from riding at home".

Australian athletes enjoyed a successful 2026 Milano Cortina Winter Olympics, including 15-year-old Indra Brown, who finished 5th in the halfpipe event. Source: AAP / Dan Himbrechts

What does the future hold for Australian snow?

Several factors contributed to this year’s historically short snow season. A spokesperson for the Bureau of Meteorology told SBS that: "Long periods with high pressure systems in the Tasman Sea occurred during winter, directing warmer air from the north over south-eastern Australia."

Dr Linden Ashcroft, a senior lecturer in climate science at the University of Melbourne, told SBS: "we just didn't get the big cold fronts, the big Antarctic blasts of cold air, as often this winter".

Not every year will be as light on snow as this year, experts say, but broader trends are concerning.

READ MORE Australia’s winter wonderland is becoming increasingly reliant on a backup plan

Also speaking to SBS, the University of Canberra’s Duanne White, associate professor in ecology and genomics, said: "there's a lot of things that go into determining how much snow we have in the mountains in any particular one year", however: "the trend is obvious".

These conditions are likely to deteriorate over the coming years, with Ashcroft saying: "We already know that next year is going to be the world's hottest on record."

"We have already locked into not having snow seasons like the seasons that maybe our parents had."

Is it too late for snow sports in Australia?

Snowboarding and downhill skiing require around 30cm of snow. Resorts must maintain this level of snow for at least 60 days a year to remain economically viable.

The use of snowmaking machines has become necessary for many resorts. But these also require cold temperatures to operate.

White explained that resorts "generate snow in a factory, effectively on site with a giant freezer, and then blow that onto the slopes," but added that "that's not exactly sustainable for a broad scale".

Perisher is among Australia's snow sports destinations facing challenges from the changing climate. Credit: Andy Kirkwood

Despite the downward trend, Ashcroft said: "It's never too late. It's never too late to stop making things get worse." Edmanson echoed this saying: "No, there's steps [people can take]".

Edmanson works with Protect Our Winters (POW), an organisation made up of climate scientists and advocates, that seeks to protect cold weather in Australia.

Modelling from POW predicts that under a "low emission scenario" Australian snow sports could still have a strong future. To reach this scenario, the organisation advocates for a "transition away from fossil fuels".

Ashcroft said: "It's not too late to save the snow, but we have to act now, and we have to act fast." However he said we "need to prepare for a future that doesn't look like the past".

Edmandon said he hopes the "next generation have the same opportunities that I do, that I had when I was a developing athlete".

"Being in the Australian Alps, is an incredible environment. It's super beautiful, and to be able to compete and train there is unreal."

title: 'Enormous interest': Coalition says exiled crown prince of Iran will visit Australia
text:
In Brief The exiled former crown prince of Iran has accepted an invitation from the Coalition to visit Australia.

The Coalition says the invitation does not mean the party supports his bid to lead the country.

Six months after United States President Donald Trump attacked Iran and called for regime change in the country, the Coalition says the exiled crown prince of Iran will visit Australia at their invitation.

Reza Pahlavi is the son of the shah of Iran, who was ousted by the Islamic Revolution. Pahlavi has lived outside Iran since 1979, and has long advocated for the fall of the current regime, positioning himself as an alternative leader for the country.

In a statement, Opposition foreign affairs spokesperson Ted O'Brien said the party's invitation to Pahlavi was not an endorsement of his leadership in Iran.

"Iran's future belongs to the Iranian people. It is not for Australia to determine who should lead Iran or what form its future government should take," O'Brien said.

The statement said the Coalition was "responding to Iranian-Australians who want their voices heard".

"We should be prepared to listen to credible voices advocating for a peaceful and democratic alternative to the regime in Tehran."

The statement said Pahlavi had accepted the Coalition's invitation to visit Australia for the first time since 1978, before his father's regime was overthrown.

The details of this visit are yet to be finalised, but the statement said Coalition MPs and senators would meet "virtually" with the former crown prince in the coming weeks "to discuss the situation in Iran, the aspirations of the Iranian people and his advocacy for a democratic transition to a secular Iran".

Engagement with Australian-Iranians

In its statement, the Coalition said the invitation had come off the back of "enormous interest from the Iranian-Australian community".

"Thousands of Persian Australians have signed our petition to bring Reza Pahlavi to Australia, Liberal MP Julian Leeser said.

READ MORE Anti-government chants heard in Iran after mass international protests

O'Brien said engagement with Iranian-Australians formed part of the Coalition's broader engagement with diaspora communities.

"For decades, the Iranian people have suffered under a brutal terrorist regime that represses its own citizens, exports terror abroad and denies its people basic freedoms."

Who is Reza Pahlavi?

After entering exile alongside his father Mohammad Reza Pahlavi — the last shah of Iran — Reza Pahlavi has become an avid supporter of opponents to Iran's ayatollahs.

Now living in the US, he has positioned himself as a person who could lead a secular, democratic Iran. He has seen his support soar in Iran and throughout the Iranian diaspora.

In January, domestic demonstrations against the regime gripped Iran, as protesters took to the streets in the thousands to protest the country's economic problems and the regime itself.

The government responded with a communications blackout and violent force against unarmed civilians. The Iranian government has said 3,100 protesters were killed during the blackout, but the United Nations has suggested the number could be as high as 20,000.

In response, Pahlavi called for a 'global day of action' in February, spurring thousands of people to rally in his support around the world.

Hundreds of thousands of people rallied globally in support of regime change in Iran in February. Source: AP / Ebrahim Noroozi

Thousands gathered in Sydney, Melbourne, Perth and Brisbane.

Pahlavi himself addressed a 250,000-person rally in Munich.

Controversially, Pahlavi has actively advocated for foreign interference in Iran. He has also faced criticism from those who question whether someone who has not lived in Iran for 50 years can legitimately position himself as a possible leader for the country.

Trump himself has expressed this concern, and despite claiming to have waged war against Iran for a variety of reasons, including regime change, Trump does not endorse Pahlavi's bid to run the country.

title: Coalition plan to hit 'gangs where it hurts' would slash tobacco tax and legalise vapes
text:
in brief The Coalition has unveiled a policy that would cut tobacco tax by 80 per cent if elected.

Vapes and nicotine pouches would also be legalised, regulated, and taxed to combat illicit sales.

Tobacco tax would be cut by as much as 80 per cent under a new Coalition plan unveiled on Wednesday.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor has outlined his plan to reduce the tax paid on purchases of cigarettes and tobacco products in an effort to reduce the lucrative nature of the illicit market.

The plan would also legalise the sale of nicotine vaping devices and nicotine pouches, which are currently restricted.

Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson said the plan will increase federal revenue while reducing cash flow to organised crime.

"It'll increase government revenue by about $2 billion a year because it will stop people buying products from the black market and will lead to them buying it in the real market," Wilson told ABC Radio National.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He argued that Labor was too focused on law enforcement while One Nation — who announced their policy of a 75 per cent reduction in tobacco duty — was too focused on cutting tax alone.

"We actually get the outcome Australians want, which is to break illegal tobacco trade, stop fuelling the fire bombings of stores ... and make sure we raise revenue to deliver a better health outcome," he said.

The Coalition has said its 80 per cent reduction plan will be backed by a $200 million nationwide crackdown on the illegal tobacco trade, which it says earns criminal gangs between $4.1 billion and $6.9 billion in profit each year.

A $60 million, three-year "public awareness and education campaign" would also be conducted to warn Australians of the dangers of smoking.

Labor Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino has previously rejected such a plan, arguing there is no evidence to show cutting taxes would eliminate the illegal trade.

Declining smoking rates under question

Public health authorities have long advocated for raising tobacco duty in an effort to price consumers out of the market. They have consistently warned that cutting taxes will reverse decades of decline in national smoking rates.

Laura Hunter, CEO of the Australian Council on Smoking and Health, previously told SBS News making cigarettes cheaper would have "huge ramifications for the health of Australians".

"Australia now has the lowest smoking rates that we've ever recorded, and that's the result of decades of policies that are designed to make cigarettes less affordable, less available in the community, and less normalised," she said.

However, the Coalition points to Australian Bureau of Statistics figures that show tobacco consumption increased by roughly 30 per cent between 2022 and 2025.

While sales of illegal cigarettes and nicotine products have declined dramatically, wastewater analysis shows that overall nicotine consumption is surging.

One study published in the JAMA Network Open journal estimated that illicit tobacco use in Australia more than doubled between 2017 and 2023.

At the same time, the cost of legal tobacco products has nearly tripled since 2016. In 2026, a standard packet of cigarettes ranges from $40 to $70, while black market cigarettes have remained at a consistent $10 to $20.

"The current approach has also become a disaster for the budget," the Opposition wrote in its press statement.

Tobacco excise has historically been one of the highest revenue earners for the Australian government, earning $16.3 billion in 2019-2020.

That figure dropped to just $8 billion last financial year, and budget estimates expect it will drop to $4 billion by the end of the decade.

Tobacco gangs waging 'economic terrorism', Opposition leader says

Rising tobacco duty has been linked to increasing incidents of gang-related violence and attacks on corner stores, particularly in the Victorian capital.

Taylor has argued that organised crime is "waging a campaign of economic terrorism on Australians".

Tobacconists such as this one in Hadfield, Melbourne, have been hit by a wave of suspicious fires potentially linked to an illicit cigarettes turf war. Source: AAP / James Ross

"Our strong plan will attack the gangs where it hurts by taking away their massive price advantage, taking away their customers, and taking away their profits," he said.

"You don’t bring organised crime to its knees by protecting its business model. You have to destroy the business model, and that’s what the Coalition's policy will do."

James Martin, associate professor in criminology at Deakin University, told SBS News that the growth of Australia's black market was primarily driven by tobacco excise increases.

He said organised crime groups had captured a growing share of the market by offering much cheaper products, while government efforts to tackle the trade through enforcement have yielded limited results.

"We've seen massive investment in law enforcement over the last few years, and it's been accompanied by record arrests, record seizures," he told SBS News.

"But the actual impacts on the market have been negligible."

Australia's Illicit Tobacco Commissioner Amber Shuhyta has warned previously that cutting tobacco excise could "pour more fuel on an already dangerous black market".

title: Missing Australians in Nepal to be pinpointed using telco data
text:
In brief Community leaders say families are united in grief as the search for survivors continues.

Fundraising and vigils are helping support those impacted by the devastating floods.

Telecommunication data is being provided to Nepali authorities to help narrow down the last known locations of Australians missing after catastrophic floods.

Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong said concerns deepen every day for the 38 Australians still unaccounted for, as the total death toll surpasses 1200.

Nepali rescue teams are expected to search in locations where many Australians are believed to have been staying, Ms Wong said during a press conference on Thursday.

The dozens of Australians are among 4200 people missing after a glacier collapse near Nepal's border with China triggered devastating floods across towns and valleys.

"I can indicate that after our inquiries that Nepali authorities have advised us that searches are being conducted in the locations identified by Australia, including [The Kailash Hotel] and the Royal Himalaya Hotel amongst others," Ms Wong said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"In both areas, army personnel are conducting searches on foot with helicopter and drone support."

Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed on Thursday that a team of specialist drone operators are being deployed to help with the effort.

The 15-person team will include members of state fire and rescue departments and will use advanced technology to provide rapid mapping and imaging.

There remains no change in the number of missing Australians. Six citizens have been confirmed safe since the disaster last Wednesday.

"Australian officials are working closely with authorities in Nepal and China to support efforts to establish their whereabouts and provide assistance to their families," Wong said.

"The conditions facing search and recovery teams remain extremely challenging.

"Communications are difficult, infrastructure has been destroyed and many areas are still difficult to reach."

Aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane arrived in Kathmandu on Wednesday, carrying humanitarian assistance and disaster relief.

More than 1,400 hygiene kits, 2,200 solar lights and phone chargers were among the items on board.

Australians have donated more than $4 million to the Emergency Action Alliance to support recovery efforts.

The federal government will provide an additional $3 million to match public donations, bringing the ongoing humanitarian support package to $11 million.

Grieving community members in Australia continue to cling to hope their loved ones are safe.

"Lots of people are stuck in the tunnels over there as well, and most don't have any contact ... we are still hopeful that maybe we can get good news," Non-Resident Nepali Association Victoria co-ordinator Mahadev Dhanuk told the Australian Associated Press (AAP).

The tight-knit Victorian Nepali community of less than 30,000 is wrapping its arms around those affected by the tragedy, with hundreds uniting at a candlelight vigil in memory of the victims in Melbourne on Monday.

"Many are not personally affected, but culturally we feel like one family. That's why everyone is devastated," Dhanuk said.

"All of the community is trying to overcome their own plight and trying to help and think how can we stand with Nepal?"

Australian families holding onto hope

On the Sunshine Coast, community members are "doing everything they can" to rally around loved ones of missing disability support worker Renee Spry.

The Queensland mother of twin daughters was returning from the religious Mount Kailash pilgrimage, at an immigration centre near the Nepal-Tibet border, minutes before the catastrophic flood swept through the area.

"Every time we hear news of another person being found alive is a moment of extraordinary joy and relief," Sunshine Coast-based Opposition foreign affairs spokesperson Ted O'Brien told AAP.

"We all, of course, on the Sunshine Coast then turn our minds to Renee and it is with hope that we think of her predicament."

The family of another missing Australian, Luke Costanzo, released a statement on Tuesday about the "unimaginably difficult situation" confronting them.

Luke Costanzo remains unaccounted for in Nepal following the deadly floods. Source: Supplied / Costanzo family

Like Spry, the 30-year-old had been visiting Tibet's Mount Kailash on a pilgrimage trek with the non-profit Isha Foundation.

"We can do nothing but continue hoping for a miracle that Luke, and the others who remain missing, are found alive and well," Costanzo's family said.

The bodies of the flood victims have begun to be buried in mass graves in Kathmandu after DNA samples were taken.

title: With falls accelerating, how far could Australia's property market drop?
text:
IN BRIEF New data has led to a shift in property market forecasts.

Major financial institutions also expect the Reserve Bank to raise interest rates for a fourth time this year.

Australia's property price downturn continues apace, with home values across the nation now 3.6 per cent below their early-2026 peak, according to new figures from property market research firm Cotality.

A sharper than expected drop has prompted major financial institutions to update their forecasts, with the Commonwealth now expecting "faster and broader" price drops than the bank had previously forecast.

Property prices peaked and began to dip from March of this year, following signals that the federal government planned to remove some tax incentives for property investors.

Interest-rate rises, supply challenges and market sentiment are also thought to have played a part in the recent downturn.

In response to the latest statistics, Housing Minister Claire O'Neil said the nation's property market was "inherently cyclical".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We see periods of really strong house price growth that are followed by a period of housing downturn — that's happened now about four times in the last decade," she told Channel Seven's Sunrise on Wednesday morning.

The median price of housing in Australia has increased by more than 400 per cent since 1999, according to recent Treasury analysis. O'Neil said that the continuation of this long-term trend would shatter aspirations for future generations.

Whilst one economist says the downturn could be the most significant in 50 years, forecasters differ on how far prices will fall, partly because of differing expectations about important factors such as interest rate changes.

Here's how to interpret the numbers.

How far have property prices already fallen?

House prices across the nation dropped by 0.9 per cent in August, according to Cotality's national Home Value Index, contributing to a 3.1 per cent fall over the winter quarter.

The drop stretches to 3.6 per cent if measured from when property prices peaked in March of this year.

Cotality also found that 93 per cent of capital city suburbs were now experiencing property price drops. That's more than double the 45.8 per cent of such suburbs that were seeing declines through 2026's autumn months.

Darwin was the only state or territory capital to buck the downward trend, recording a 0.6 per cent increase over the last month and 0.9 per cent over the quarter.

At the other end of the spectrum, prices are falling fastest in Sydney, with home values decreasing by 1.4 per cent in August and 4.7 per cent across the quarter.

How far could property prices fall?

The Commonwealth Bank is now expecting prices to fall by around 9 per cent nationwide from a March 2026 peak before bottoming out in April 2027.

Australia's largest bank is also forecasting more significant drops in larger state capitals, with Sydney and Melbourne predicted to see declines of 13 and 12 per cent, respectively.

It's a significant shift from the bank's pre-winter predictions that dwelling prices would largely flatline over the course of the year.

CommBank also predicts that property prices will start rising again after April, eventually increasing by 2 per cent over the calendar year. The figure is a far cry from the 9.2 per cent property price went up across the country in 2025.

AMP is predicting a slightly steeper drop, with chief economist Shane Oliver saying that he now expects prices to fall by around 10 per cent across Australia.

Like the Commonwealth, Oliver also said drops would be most pronounced in large capitals like Sydney, noting that prices across Australia's largest property market had already dropped by 7.1 per cent since their peak in February.

Before the latest price-movement data from Cotality, NAB was forecasting a national drop of around 7 per cent, with declines of around 10 per cent in Sydney and Melbourne balanced by dips of between 2-4 per cent across smaller capital cities.

The bank's 10 August outlook paper also reminded readers that these declines were "broadly in line" with those seen in 2018-2019 and those caused by the Reserve Bank's rate-tightening round of 2022-2023.

Independent property economist Cameron Kusher told SBS News that he expects price drops will end up "on the higher side of the consensus 8-11 per cent".

"Most major banks and forecasters, myself included, believe that this downturn is going to be the largest downturn in the past 50 years or so," he said.

"As to whether specific forecasts are accurate, it's very hard to get these things right, but the trajectory of the housing market is clearly lower and with falls accelerating."

He said the fall in prices was being driven by an influx of sellers while some buyers were biding their time.

"At the moment, most would-be buyers are not in a hurry to make a purchase and [are] waiting for prices to fall further. How long that continues will also factor into how far prices fall."

However, he said the key determinant of how far prices would drop would be how much higher interest rates go and how long they remain elevated.

How many more interest rate rises will we see?

While property prices might be falling, inflation remains high in other areas of the economy, and most banks and economists predict the central bank will hike rates at one of its board's three remaining meetings of 2026.

The Commonwealth is predicting a 0.25 per cent hike at its early November meeting, although it believes a late September hike remains a possibility.

It predicts the Reserve Bank will only start cutting rates in May next year.

Similarly, AMP also expects another rate hike in November, with September also a possibility.

The Reserve Bank's cash rate has been raised three times already this year and currently sits at 4.35 per cent.

Kusher told SBS News that he thinks it would be at least 12 months before the RBA could start considering interest rate cuts.

Thulo Bharkhu, Nepal: It is the first day of Buddhist mourning in the heartbroken village of Thulo Bharkhu, and a grandmother is weeping by two photos she has fixed to her dresser. They show Santu Tamang, the only one of her six children to attend university, dressed sharply in a blazer, smiling beside his wife, Pasang. In the other frame, Yanin, 3, is sat rugged up against the cold, his little sister, Bhechen, cosied between his legs. On paper, they are missing, but Dawa Yangji Tamang, 66, knows they are dead. Too many days have passed now. Nepalese rescuers sifting the river banks and obliterated villages along the Trishuli River are finding body parts, not survivors. So Dawa lights candles under photos from the family’s recent holiday to the capital of Kathmandu, and cries. “I have lost my will to live,” she says. Dawa Yangji Tamang mourns the loss of her son, her daughter-in-law and her grandchildren. All four were claimed by the flash floods that have devastated areas at the Nepal-Tibet border. Kate Geraghty Thulo Bharkhu village, built onto a mountainside in Nepal’s stunning Himalayas, lost 22 sons and daughters on Wednesday last week when a glacial collapse near the border with Tibet sent an inland tidal wave tearing down the Trishuli River.

Advertisement

The Ghewa ceremony being carried out for bus driver Karma Waleya Tamang, who is believed to have perished while ferrying passengers back from the Tibet border. Kate Geraghty Residents of Thulo Bharkhu, a hamlet that lost 22 people in the floods, pray for their deceased loved ones even as the search continues to recover their bodies. Kate Geraghty The dead had been working out of town along the river corridor, providing for their families. Those families, 12 households in total, are now performing the first of what will be a year-long series of rituals to send their loved ones peacefully to the next life. Ordinarily, the bodies would have been cremated soon after death. Families mourn their own, then go up the street to help other families mourn theirs. No one is talking about miracles. The rituals mark an acceptance, and they are accepting together. They serve calorific cups of a local tea made with salt, wildflower and yak butter. In Tamang culture, when people eat at funeral rituals, called Ghewa, they are also eating for the dead. The families, ever warm, insist everyone, including this masthead, eats and drinks their fill. Dawa’s son Santu, an engineer, was the pride of the family. For a time, he had even worked in Japan. When a job came up at the Rasuwagadhi hydro plant, one of many stations harnessing Nepal’s snow-fed rivers, he moved his family there. Santu’s relatives believe he died at work. Pasang and the children would have been taken at home.

Advertisement

Dawa was on a video call with the kids only the day before. They were chirping “amma”, she says – the Nepali word for grandmother With luck, she will get their bodies. Nepal has called for international help with processing DNA and testing. For now, marked body bags are being buried in mass graves in Chitwan district. Some are going in ambulances and police buses. Anyone caught within a dozen vehicles behind will know because of the smell. Hundreds of bodies and parts have washed all the way into India. The ones recovered in Nepal are coming out of ruins or being picked out of the muddy banks. It’s possible thousands are buried under the freshly laid quicksand. Nepalese police carry bodies to a helicopter for a flight to Chitwan, where hundreds of disaster victims are being buried. Kate Geraghty A woman among destroyed buildings in Betrawoti, which was severely affected by the Nepal flash flood that has killed more than a thousand people. Thousands are still missing. Kate Geraghty The market town of Betrawoti has been swallowed up by a deluge of mud. Many of its buildings have been destroyed. Kate Geraghty Only at river level can you appreciate the volume of water the people were up against. Steep mountainsides at the narrow passes are sheared clean of any vegetation 50 metres above the present river level.

Advertisement

It will grow back. Bridges will be rebuilt, eventually. But the damage to villages such as Thulo Bharkhu will last. The pain extends beyond borders and ocean, linking this small, unknown village with a profound grief being felt on many shores. At the most recent count, 36 Australians are feared dead. Mendo Lapachi, who lost her brother and two sisters-in-law, reacts to talking of her family and the flood as she gets ready to hold the Ghewa ceremony. Kate Geraghty Destroyed buildings in Betrawoti. Kate Geraghty Chogyal Dorje Lama is holding a Ghewa for his wife, Pratima, his brother Thile and sister-in-law Chenku. All three were killed in Syabrubesi, about a kilometre away on the banks of the Trishuli. Chogyal’s wife, the deputy mayor, managed one final call to her husband as the river bore down. “She was saying, ‘My mother, my mother, mother,’” he says. It is Nepalese equivalent of “my god”. Chogyal says it sounded like she was running. “Then the voice was gone,” he says. “That voice is still coming to my head. How can I forget?” He gazes mournfully at Pratima’s framed portrait resting low on a coffee table, recalling the community work she did for children and the elderly, how she was made to run for deputy mayor by insistent locals.

Advertisement

The couple were just about to try for a family. “Now, I am alone. So how to live?” Chogyal asks. Chogyal Dorje Lama sits near photos of his wife, Pratima Tamang (right), who was a nurse and deputy mayor of the local council and was in an office building in Syabrubesi when the floods hit. Kate Geraghty Syabrubesi is best known as the starting point of the Langtang Valley trek. It is also a stopover for Hindu pilgrims on their way north to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash. Chogyal’s brother owned one of Syabrubesi’s hotels, the Royal Himalayan, and was probably inside with Chenku and guests as it was swept away at about 9am. The hotel was fully booked with 70 to 80 people the night before the flood, Chogyal believes. At least four of the guests were Australians. Sydney’s Sreedharan Iyer, 53, his wife, Lakshmi, 49, and the couple’s two sons, Rishab, 23, and Rudhra, 20, were travelling as part of a group of 15 Australian pilgrims, most of whom stayed the night before the tragedy at the Hotel Kailash, close to the border. That hotel was swept away, too. The pilgrims are part of a wider group of Australians caught up in the tragedy.

title: De Minaur dumped from US Open in straight sets as Kyrgios cocaine ban revealed
text:
Advertisement

SportTennisUS Open De Minaur dumped from US Open in straight sets as Kyrgios cocaine ban revealed Marc McGowan Updated September 4, 2026 — 1:41pm ,first published September 4, 2026 — 8:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex de Minaur could relinquish his top-10 ranking within weeks after a second-round US Open defeat capped his least-successful grand slam season in three years. The world No.7 suffered a 6-4, 7-5, 6-2 loss to dangerous Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp in New York on Friday (AEST), continuing a prolonged form downturn after a brilliant start to his 2026 campaign. Loading De Minaur’s disappointing exit came on a dramatic day at Flushing Meadows, where wildcard Dane Sweeny was the sole Australian to progress to the round of 32 after toppling fancied Italian Lorenzo Musetti. It also happened as Nick Kyrgios accepted a one-month suspension for out-of-competition use of cocaine.

Advertisement

“My level today wasn’t good enough. It’s pretty straightforward,” de Minaur said. “I gave myself every chance by being competitive, having a good mindset, a good attitude, but it was just one of those days when the feeling of the ball on the strings wasn’t there. De Minaur stretches for a forehand. AP Photo/Frank Franklin II “I was making a lot of errors, which is not really my normal game style. I can’t really explain the reasoning of it, but it felt like the more I tried, the more intensity, the more fired up I was getting, I just kept on making unforced errors … [it was] a tough day at the office.” De Minaur lost this early in a major only twice in his past 13 events.

Advertisement

He advanced to a second Australian Open quarter-final in January, but bowed out in the third and fourth rounds at Roland-Garros and Wimbledon, respectively. De Minaur reached the US Open quarter-finals the past two years, and his defeat – his earliest in New York in five years – means wildcard Sweeny is the only Australian still in singles contention. Alex de Minaur suffered a disappointing second-round loss at the US Open. Getty Images Sweeny, a 170-centimetre battler ranked 123 in the world, is celebrating his maiden top-20 victory, taking down Italy’s dual grand slam semi-finalist Musetti 3-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-2 in a titanic upset to reach the third round for the first time. It is van de Zandschulp’s second major scalp at the US Open after eliminating Carlos Alcaraz in the same round two years ago, but he had never beaten de Minaur in four prior meetings.

Advertisement

The result was an upset on paper only, given power-hitting van de Zandschulp entered the tournament in better form than de Minaur, who has made it beyond the quarter-finals at any event only once since February. The 27-year-old was crestfallen after his Wimbledon defeat to Flavio Cobolli in July, saying afterwards that not stepping up on that stage “breaks me inside”. He played down his devastated post-match reaction in Washington a few weeks later, but has struggled on court since. Australia’s Dane Sweeny is breaking new ground at this year’s US Open. AP Photo/Seth Wenig De Minaur’s much-scrutinised serve failed him against van de Zandschulp, committing seven double faults compared to only four aces, while conceding 11 break points and dropping serve five times. He hit one of those double faults to go a set and 4-3 down, but a stroke of fortune in the next game could have proven a turning point. After some fabulous defence, a de Minaur backhand clipped the net cord and whizzed past van de Zandschulp for a winner to reduce him to 15-40.

Advertisement

De Minaur drew level, then edged ahead, but lost a marathon service game at 5-5 after saving four break points before conceding on the fifth. Van de Zandschulp apologised because a mishit ball landed short in the court to drag de Minaur into the net and create his forehand pass opportunity, but the Australian could have done more. The Dutchman went two sets up, and the odds were against de Minaur, who had never erased that deficit in 27 attempts. After going off court between sets, de Minaur tried to up the ante, but flayed a forehand long in the third game to drop serve. Two break-back points came and went in the next game before van de Zandschulp broke his top-10 rival once more to as good as seal the Aussie’s fate. Little has happened easily for Sweeny in his until-now off-Broadway tennis career, so he was due some good fortune – and it is coming in spades at this US Open.

Advertisement

Musetti spent most of the final three sets physically struggling, hunched over in the corner of the court and generally looking under the weather. He took an off-court medical timeout after going 3-0 down in the third set, and showed the odd sign of life, but Sweeny never let up. Sweeny’s only previous match against this calibre of opponent was a straight-sets defeat to American star Ben Shelton in the second round at this year’s Australian Open. He is now guaranteed a payday of more than $400,000, and is provisionally at a career-high live ranking of No.109 ahead of another on-court date with a seeded Italian, Luciano Darderi. “I’m so grateful to be able to even compete in grand slams,” Sweeny said. Loading

Advertisement

“I put a lot of work in. The tennis journey is such a rollercoaster, and I’m so incredibly grateful to play in front of an awesome crowd and to soak up this moment. To win, and to get a couple of wins, is awesome.” This milestone moment comes barely two years since Sweeny took a multi-month break from the sport after suffering through a form slump, just as he felt close to finally breaking through into elite company. “That’s the beautiful thing about pursuing something so hard like tennis,” he said. “Tennis can change on the flip of a coin. You’ve just got to keep persevering, and that’s what I did. I wasn’t getting results for a long while, but there’s a law of probability. I knew it was somehow going to swing in my favour if I just kept going, and I did. “Now I’m here, and it’s the best decision I ever made to come back after that two months.”

Advertisement

Australia’s Nick Kyrgios served a one-month ban for using cocaine. AP Meanwhile, the International Tennis Integrity Agency announced on Friday morning that Kyrgios had accepted a one-month suspension for out-of-competition use of cocaine, while agreeing to enter a treatment program that reduces the ban from three months. Kyrgios apologised to his family, friends and fans last month for making a “huge mistake” when his provisional suspension was revealed. He admitted to the ITIA that he used cocaine socially on a night out before he competed in Mallorca. Kyrgios’ suspension officially ended on Thursday, subject to him completing his treatment program, and he forfeited his prizemoney and ranking points from the Mallorca event. Former doubles partner Stefanos Tsitsipas, whom Kyrgios has feuded with, said after his first-round US Open victory that the news did not surprise him and that he was aware of the situation.

Advertisement

Alexei Popyrin is out of the US Open in the second round. AP Photo/Andres Kudacki For a while, a second Australian underdog seemed poised to upset a highly ranked Italian as qualifier Tristan Schoolkate snatched the first set from Roland-Garros finalist Cobolli, only to go down 3-6, 6-3, 6-4, 7-5 to the No.5 seed. A dispirited Alexei Popyrin also exited the US Open, losing 2-6, 7-6 (7-4), 7-6 (7-3), 6-2 to 25th-seeded Chilean left-hander Alejandro Tabilo after a bright start. The Musetti result continued some overdue luck for Sweeny, who was supposed to contest US Open qualifying, but several player withdrawals enabled Popyrin to make the main draw cut-off, and transferred Tennis Australia’s reciprocal wildcard to him. The 25-year-old parlayed his wildcard into his first grand slam win outside Melbourne Park when Frenchman Corentin Moutet retired with an arm injury while trailing 7-6 (7-4), 6-4, 3-0.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Drugs in sport It’s been said Kyrgios is ‘not good for the sport’ of tennis. It’s never been that simple Marc McGowan Sports reporter Musetti was dressed head-to-toe in sponsored Asics gear, whereas the mustachioed Sweeny wore a plain white shirt and red cap to shade him from the harsh and humid New York heat. The war wounds on Sweeny’s elbows and knees were evidence of his scrappy style, too. Everything changed after a relatively routine opening set, albeit one Sweeny had chances in. Musetti began looking off-colour during the second set, which he lost in lopsided fashion, and never fully recovered despite glimpses of his usual spectacular shot-making. Like the second set, Musetti quickly handed over a pair of breaks in the third.

Advertisement

He twice recovered a break, only to hand it straight back to Sweeny, whose relentless hitting and scampering never wavered. The fourth set took a similar path as Musetti gifted an immediate break of serve that left him playing catch up again. On a day of upsets, third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime also departed in four sets to Karen Khachanov, but Coco Gauff, Iga Swiatek, Taylor Fritz and Naomi Osaka were among the winners. title: ‘Crisis situation’: Volkswagen to cut another 50,000 jobs as it fights to survive
text:

BusinessCompaniesCars ‘Crisis situation’: Volkswagen to cut another 50,000 jobs as it fights to survive William Wilkes September 4, 2026 — 1:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Volkswagen’s supervisory board backed a sweeping overhaul that calls for 50,000 additional job cuts, far fewer models and a smaller industrial footprint, giving chief executive officer Oliver Blume his clearest mandate yet to remake Europe’s biggest carmaker. The plan doubles workforce reductions agreed to across Volkswagen Group brands since late 2024, while also paving the way for the company to slim its vehicle line-up by as much as 50 per cent by 2035. The 50,000 new cuts represent about 8 per cent of VW’s global workforce as of the end of last year. The plan doubles workforce reductions agreed to across Volkswagen Group brands since late 2024, while also paving the way for the company to slim its vehicle lineup by as much as 50 per cent by 2035. Jochen Luebke “Given intensifying global competition, shifting demand and technological change in the automotive industry, a consistent alignment of workforce capacity with economic reality is essential,” the company said in a statement. The board approved the comprehensive restructuring effort, known as the Future Plan, at a meeting in Wolfsburg, Germany. VW’s works council, which represents the company’s employees, sought to temper the potential for job losses, saying the 50,000 figure is a planning assumption derived from Volkswagen’s target to achieve a 9 per cent margin by 2030 rather than a fixed headcount goal. A spokesman for the labour group also said that compulsory layoffs at Volkswagen remain ruled out through the end of 2030 under existing agreements.

Advertisement

That distinction reflects the broader compromise behind the unanimous board vote, reached a day earlier than initially expected after weeks of increasingly bitter rhetoric. Labour representatives had accepted that Volkswagen needed further cost reductions. But they fiercely opposed plant closures, moves to weaken co-determination – Germany’s system of worker representation in corporate decisions – and plans to separate parts of the core VW business. VW’s US depositary receipts jumped about 9 per cent in New York on Thursday, the most since March 2023. Chief executive officer Oliver Blume has been given his clearest mandate yet to remake Europe’s biggest carmaker. Bloomberg In the final package, Blume won backing for the extra job cuts and sweeping efficiency measures. Workers secured assurances that no factory would be immediately abandoned and that contentious site decisions would instead be worked through over the coming months. The agreement gives the CEO stronger backing to push ahead as VW struggles with high costs, weak demand and intensifying competition, particularly from Chinese carmakers. The deal stops short of immediately closing factories. VW acknowledged that it currently has about 500,000 vehicles-worth of excess annual capacity in Europe. The company said its factories in Emden, Hannover, Neckarsulm and Zwickau currently lack competitive future production plans once existing models phase out between 2031 and 2034. Alternative uses for the plants will now be explored, Volkswagen said.

Advertisement

That gave labour-friendly board members room to support the overhaul without abandoning core red lines. IG Metall chief Christiane Benner and works council head Daniela Cavallo said the compromise had “prevented a dangerous escalation”, while stressing that no plant closing had been agreed upon and that plans to separate the VW passenger-car and components businesses were off the table. “The work is only just beginning,” the labour chiefs said of the restructuring plan. “What we will continue never to accept, however, is the burden being placed one-sidedly on employees.” Benner said the carmaker was dealing with a “crisis situation”. Related Article Pharmaceuticals Ozempic’s maker is in trouble. Tablets may be the answer The Porsche-Piëch family, which controls a majority of VW’s voting rights through Porsche SE, has pushed for faster action as returns and dividend flows come under pressure. Blume has argued that Volkswagen can no longer afford to carry the same sprawling cost base and industrial footprint while funding investments in electric vehicles, batteries and software. Porsche SE “welcomes this decision and intends to continue to support the transformation efforts of the board of management of its core investment, Volkswagen AG,” a spokesperson for Porsche SE said in a statement.

Advertisement

The overhaul targets an operating margin of 9 per cent by 2030 on annual sales of about 9 million vehicles. VW is also planning €135 billion of capital expenditure and research and development spending over 2027 through 2031, the company said. Checking in Gold Coast Airport is a breeze, with both domestic and international services in the same terminal. I’m on board the airline’s inaugural flight on this route – from one holiday destination to another – which creates a buzz at check-in. The smiles are wide (staff), the shirts are loud (passengers), and white linen is the order of the day (even this reviewer understood the assignment). Baggage Sign up for the Traveller newsletter The latest travel news, tips and inspiration delivered to your inbox. Sign up now. The airline’s “Value” fare allows one personal item, one carry-on bag up to seven kilograms, and one checked bag up to 30 kilograms. The cheapest “Lite” fare does not include checked baggage and comes with a hefty fee (more than $250 for a return flight to Nadi on this route) if you want to add it. The Value fare is much better value (about $50 more return to Nadi) if you have a checked bag. Loyalty scheme Fiji Airways has adopted the American Airlines AAdvantage travel rewards program, which allows points to be earned towards the loyalty programs of Oneworld partners. You can also book flights with the airline via Qantas, including on Frequent Flyer points, through a code-share agreement. Fiji Airways’ Tabua Club is a subscription-based program (not a points program) that provides a few perks such as additional baggage and lounge access at selected airports. The seat

There’s a decent amount of legroom in the 737 MAX 8’s economy cabin. With 162 economy seats arranged in a 3-3 configuration, the cabin feels less crowded than wide-body layouts. Though the 17-inch width (43 centimetres) and 5-inch (13 centimetres) recline is standard MAX 8 territory, the pitch (legroom) is a decent 32 inches (81 centimetres). With Lite or Value fares there’s an additional charge ($16) to select your preferred standard seat. I take my chances, scoring an aisle with an empty seat beside me. Entertainment and tech As more airlines ditch seat-back entertainment in favour of streaming to personal devices, a 10-inch (25 centimetre) touch screen is a welcome sight – until I scroll through the movies and TV series and fail to find anything new or appealing. Even the “Fresh on board” movies are stale. Fortunately the magazine section is good and I’ve brought a book. There’s a USB port for charging, and Wi-Fi can be purchased for $US7.95 ($11.30) for browsing or $US14.95 ($21.20) for light streaming. Forget the free “unlimited chat”. Service

Smiles all around from the crew. This is where Fiji Airways shines. Staff are relaxed, friendly and unfailingly helpful. The most memorable part? Every interaction comes with a smile; the genuine kind, not the forced version you often see elsewhere. The holiday starts here. Food The economy class chicken curry. Kerry van der Jagt An hour into our flight we’re offered a full meal service, which makes for a late lunch (2.30pm) given our delayed departure. I opt for the chicken curry, which is tender and flavoursome (a tofu-based vegetarian dish is the second option). Served with rice and accompanied by a pasta salad, bread roll and a white mousse for dessert, it’s decent fare, but I’d love to see some fresh salad or vegetables. Sustainability Guided by the Fijian philosophy of maroroya (“to protect”), the airline has invested in a modern fleet that delivers up to 25 per cent fuel savings over previous-generation aircraft. SkyBreathe software tracks and minimises fuel consumption. For every take-off, a mangrove tree is planted; there are 98,000 new trees to date.* One more thing Fiji Airways has just launched FlyWell – a wellness program designed to improve passenger and crew wellbeing that it claims is the first of its kind. The program, available to business class passengers flying from Fiji to the US in June and July, features wearable technology aimed at improving circulation and adjusting circadian rhythms, along with wellness treatments available at the airline’s premium lounge in Nadi. title: An $1080 share investment I made in 1993 is now worth $204,000. Should I sell?
text:
I have about 1300 Commbank shares. l started off with 200 in 1993 and have just kept going with the dividend reinvestment plan. With the tax changes coming in July 2027, should l be selling them before that date? I am 65, my wife is 66,and we plan to retire at about that time. We have no debt and a reasonable sum in each of our super funds.

That $1080 investment you made back in 1993 is now worth $204,000. Simon Letch

The most important ingredient to investment and wealth creation success is patience, something most of us struggle with. So firstly, a big “well done” for sitting on these shares for more than 30 years. That $1080 investment you made back in 1993 is now worth $204,000, a fantastic outcome, and a great illustration of the wisdom of investing into productive businesses via shares.

There are several reasons why you might choose to sell these shares – to boost your super on retirement, to help a family member, to buy a caravan and hit the road, and I’m sure there is plenty more. But selling them because of the tax changes coming in 2027 is not one of them.

From July next year the way capital gains tax is calculated will change. But that change only affects the period from 1 July 2027 onwards. It has no impact on your tax treatment up to that point. This change is therefore in no way a catalyst to induce a sale that you otherwise would not have made.

Step 1 Season the beef with salt and pepper.

Step 2 In a large, heavy-based dutch oven or pot, heat 1 tablespoon of the olive oil over a high heat and brown the beef in batches. Remove the beef from the pot and lower the heat to medium.

Step 3 Add the remaining olive oil and brown the shallots or onions. Add the garlic and cook for a minute further or until fragrant, then add all the spices and bay leaves and cook for 1 minute, stirring well to coat. Add the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute.

title: This $800 Dyson toothbrush is selling out. But is it really worth the hype?
text:
Advertisement

LifestyleHealth & wellnessOral health This $800 Dyson toothbrush is selling out. But is it really worth the hype? Shona Hendley September 4, 2026 — 12:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Have you ever wanted to see what your dentist sees? While many of us would probably answer no, a product that allows you to do just that – the Dyson CameraJet electric toothbrush – has hit the market. And it’s causing quite the buzz. Dyson’s foray into oral care, touted as the “complete oral care routine in one toothbrush”, includes an array of functions, including jet washing, liquid flossing and mouthwash dispensing. Retailing at $799, the Dyson CameraJet electric toothbrush can show you things you’ve never seen before (and may never want to see again). But along with the hefty $799 price tag, it’s the integrated 100k-pixel macro-lens camera that is attracting the most attention. This feature, which Dyson says can detect, track and predict gaps between teeth in real time, is also said to remove “up to 72 per cent more plaque than market-leading electric toothbrushes” by delivering a targeted jet of mouthwash to the detected area.

Advertisement

This mouthwash, along with toothpaste, needs to be non- or low-foaming, so the camera can see clearly. The brand has launched its own line of these products, retailing at $15.99 each. Dyson says these features – including an app which gives you feedback on your brushing, after analysing footage – set the CameraJet apart. But are people willing to fork out almost $800 on a toothbrush and, most importantly, what do dentists think? Do people really want it? From the brand that has generated cult followings for many of its products, from cordless vacuums to the Dyson Airwrap, you’d assume this could follow suit. At the time of publishing, the CameraJet is out of stock on the Dyson Australia website but available from other retailers, including JB Hi-Fi, The Good Guys and Harvey Norman. However, exact sales figures in Australia remain unconfirmed.

Advertisement

Related Article Wellness Is your beloved sparkling water damaging your teeth? “Dyson does not comment on specific sales performance. But we’re delighted by the initial response and engagement we’ve seen from consumers so far,” says Niamh Turney, a senior engineer and commercial manager at Dyson. On social media, led by influencers, gadget reviewers and users from the dental industry, #dysontoothbrush has accumulated over 600,000 posts on TikTok, while Instagram has seen mixed reactions, including jokes about the live-stream feature and outrage over the product’s cost. What do dentists think? Dr Monica Farrelly, a dentist and Oral Health Promoter for the Australian Dental Association, says much of the hype is likely attributable to the brand rather than the product itself.

Advertisement

“Dyson entering a completely new category always draws coverage,” she says, adding that the “novelty factor” of a toothbrush with a camera and the product’s price point may also have contributed. Feature-wise, Farrelly believes it is too early to say with confidence whether the product deserves the attention or the price tag. The product’s conical jet is said to be more effective and gentler on gums than other water flossers. “Independent, peer-reviewed clinical research on the CameraJet specifically doesn’t exist yet, since the product has only just launched,” she says. However, she says that “the underlying idea – a toothbrush that helps people clean interdental gaps more consistently – is genuinely useful because interdental cleaning is where most people fall short.”

Advertisement

“Whether the camera and AI targeting deliver meaningfully better results than a person using a water flosser or interdental brushes properly is not yet established,” she adds. Editor's pick Fertility Single at 30, Chloe decided to freeze her eggs. She wasn’t prepared for what came next She also has some reservations about the camera being used by people without dental training. “It may be difficult for people to know what they are looking at: is it plaque, calculus or a hole?” Farrelly says. “The camera itself also only shows you limited surfaces of the teeth. Even as dentists, we need to take X-rays to accurately detect all things in the mouth.” Dr Giulia D’Anna, principal dentist at iDental, says most of the features of the product that look good are the usual features of an electric toothbrush.

Advertisement

“A small round oscillating head is good at being able to target small spaces well, with minimal movement required from the user,” she says. “This means hard-to-reach areas are better brushed.” What to look for in a toothbrush When looking for and choosing an electric toothbrush, D’Anna says that in addition to the small head size, she recommends: A pressure sensor that alerts when you’re brushing too hard

A 30-second timer function. She recommends 30 seconds of brushing for the lower outside, lower inside, upper inner and upper outer segments – so two minutes total “These features are generally included in a brush that retails for around $120 to $180,” D’Anna explains.

Advertisement

Farrelly says that individual factors – age, orthodontic appliances such as braces, gum conditions such as recession – should be considered when choosing an electric or non-electric toothbrush, as people with sensitive teeth or gums benefit from soft bristles or a gentle brushing mode if using an electric brush. According to Farrelly, manual brushes are often perfectly adequate, though older adults or people with reduced hand dexterity often do best with an electric toothbrush with large, easy-to-grip handles. title: Coles cuts ties with controversial US giant after Aussie outcry: 'Right call'
text:
Following a public outcry to cut ties with US tech giant Palantir, Coles has confirmed it will be ending its contract with the data company.

Coles had previously defended its relationship with Palantir, but on Friday confirmed to Yahoo News the supermarket will not extend its contract past 2027.

"Coles and Palantir have agreed to conclude their partnership after three years of collaboration," the supermarket told Yahoo News on Friday.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The supermarket chain declined to comment on the value of the partnership or on why it has decided to end the contract.

The two companies had been working together since early 2024.

Palantir was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel. It develops software for companies and government agencies to analyse vast amounts of data.

Critics had been suspicious of Palantir's involvement with the supermarket, given its history of supplying tracking software to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the military.

Coles has denied passing customer surveillance data to Palantir in the past and insisted it uses the US company's software only for operational planning and analysis.

After calls for Coles to end its controversial partnership with American tech giant Palantir, the supermarket has now cut ties with the company.

Get Up applauds the termination of the Coles-Palantir contract

Political activist group GetUp had petitioned Coles to end its partnership, a petition signed by more than 83,000 people.

Interim GetUp CEO Paul Ferris is welcoming the ending of the relationship.

"Credit where it's due: ending this contract is the right call for Coles' customers and workers, and we welcome it," he said.

Coles and Palantir defend partnership

While Coles transitions from its partnership with Palantir, a spokesperson said the technology the US company had provided was valuable, "particularly in rostering, store operations and supply chain planning".

"Coles uses this software as a data integration and analytics software platform, which helps our team members make practical, informed decisions across our business," a spokesperson said.

"The software is used for bakery production planning, trading performance analysis and rostering. It's an operational platform focused on helping stores run more effectively."

"The software is deployed within Coles' own environment and is operated and isolated under Coles controls.

Palantir 'proud' to work with Coles

A Palantir spokesperson told Yahoo News in August the company is "proud" its software is helping Coles and denied the claims that the technology is being used for surveillance.

"Our focus with Coles is straightforward - we help the business become more data-driven and more efficient in the decisions it makes every day," the spokesperson said.

They reiterated that the software supports bakery production planning, promotion evaluation, rostering, and retail media performance reporting.

He said the company has "no interest" in mining, scraping or monetising data.

"We simply help organisations use their own data," he said.

"Coles' software is fully segregated, isolated, and secure, exactly as it is for every customer we work with. Legally and contractually, Coles owns its data, that data never leaves Coles' control, and there is no central system pooling the data of Australian shoppers."

title: Petting zoo breaks silence after 3yo dies
text:
A petting zoo in Victoria's southeast has broken its silence after a three-year-old girl died and a young boy was hospitalised after visiting the farm, where it's believed they contracted a rare and life-threatening infection.

The girl spent the past six weeks in intensive care at Monash Children's Hospital after contracting the illness.

It caused permanent brain damage and kidney failure, with her family confirming her death in a GoFundMe update on Monday.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"We've lost our darling girl," the family wrote.

A three-year-old died after contracting a rare infection. Picture: GoFundMe

The little girl died after contracting Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) – a rare and life-threatening illness that can cause kidney and brain damage from shiga toxin-producing Escherichia cold (STEC) bacteria.

STEC is commonly found across farms in the guts and faeces of animals, particularly cows, with more than 1000 cases reported every year, according to the Centre for Disease Control.

Symptoms can include diarrhoea, vomiting and nausea, with symptoms often showing three or four days after being infected.

It's believed the girl picked up the bacteria while visiting the petting zoo, where another child was also hospitalised after attending a birthday party at the same location.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The owners of the petting zoo have since told NewsWire they were deeply upset by the girl's death.

"We would just like to express our deepest and sincere condolences to the family and friends of the young girl who has passed away," they told NewsWire.

There has been an increase in STEP cases over the past three years. Picture: NewsWire / Bianca De Marchi

Increase in STEP cases

The Victorian Department of Health launched an investigation into the STEC outbreak in August.

On Thursday, deputy chief health officer Clare Looker extended her "deepest condolences to this young child's family members as they continue to grieve the devastating loss of their loved one".

"The Department of Health investigates all reported cases of haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) to identify potential sources of infection and prevent further cases," Dr Looker said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"These infections can occasionally lead to haemolytic uraemic syndrome, particularly in young children and people who are immunocompromised."

Patrons of petting zoos and farms have been told to throughly wash their hands after handling animals.

Dr Looker said there had been an increase in STEC notifications in the past three years as laboratory testing increased and improved.

"When we do investigate this case particularly, we ask about a whole range of exposures because unfortunately this STEP bacteria is very common in our environment," she said.

"We find it in lots of animals, in lots of different environmental contaminations."

While farms and petting zoos are responsible for providing patrons with information and hygiene facilities to reduce infection, parents have also been warned to supervise their children around animals.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The petting zoo owners said they had been working with health officials and would step up their measures to prevent further incidents.

"We have followed (health officials') advice and increased signage promoting handwashing and good hygiene and added additional handwash stations around the farm," they said.

The petting zoo will not shut down after the incidents. Picture: iStock

Petting zoo to remain open

Dr Looker said since the bacteria was found in most farms and petting zoo environments, there would be no reason to shut the petting zoo.

"We know this bacteria exists in many farms, so I don't think that shutting a single farm that is taking all the right public health protective measures to stop the risk for children of the community, so at this stage there's no consideration," she said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Dr Looker said the department worked closely with petting zoos to ensure "they've got very good handwashing facilities".

"We've got lots of signage available to ensure people can have supervised handwashing with soap and water, not just hand sanitiser, and that people are made aware of the importance of that, particularly when they're in contact with animals," she said.

"We work very closely with the council to help make sure it's communicated to the residents."
